# CLIO Coder

> CLIO Coder is the open-source meta-harness for scientific software: every model you have, behind shared project guidance and checks you can inspect. Use it in the terminal or the desktop alpha with local or cloud models. Apache 2.0.

CLIO Coder reads, edits, and runs checks in your repository. It records what passed, what failed, and what was never checked. Connect a local model server, an institutional endpoint, a subscription, or a cloud API, and switch models with one command. The installer needs no root and works on HPC login nodes.

- Install on macOS, Linux, or WSL: `curl -fsSL https://coder.iowarp.ai/install.sh | sh`
- Install with npm (Node.js 22.19 or newer): `npm install -g @iowarp/clio-coder`
- Connect a model in a project: `clio-coder configure`; then run `clio-coder` for the terminal or `clio-coder gui --open` for the desktop alpha.
- Current release: v0.8.0. Source: https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder. License: Apache 2.0.

This file holds the public CLIO Coder guides (documentation for v0.8.0), tutorials, and research pages as Markdown. Each section names the page it comes from.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs.html

# Install CLIO Coder

Install, update, and launch CLIO Coder on your machine.

## Install

You need a model with tool calling. Linux, macOS and WSL are the primary platforms; native Windows is best effort. Every command below installs the latest release. Choose the tab for your system.

### macOS, Linux and WSL

```sh
curl -fsSL https://coder.iowarp.ai/install.sh | sh
```

The installer brings its own Node.js 24 and needs no root, including on x64 HPC login nodes with glibc 2.17 or newer. It checks the Node download against its published SHA-256 checksums, and their OpenPGP signature when `gpg` is installed. It installs under `~/.local/share/clio-coder-install` on Linux or `~/Library/Application Support/clio-coder/install` on macOS, and writes the launcher `~/.local/bin/clio-coder`.

On Linux, an install run from a terminal ends by offering the desktop app, which starts at login and appears in your app menu. The optional Claude Agent SDK, about 224 MB, is skipped; CLIO Coder offers to fetch it the first time you need it.

Pass options after `sh -s --`. For example, `--modify-path` adds the launcher directory to your shell profile, `--gui` sets up the desktop app without asking, and `--include-claude-sdk` installs the SDK now:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://coder.iowarp.ai/install.sh | sh -s -- --modify-path
```

On a cluster, read [Install on a cluster](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/hpc-clusters.html).

### PowerShell

Native Windows is best effort, so use the current stable release. Install, repair, rollback and uninstall were checked by hand on an earlier release, on one x64 machine with PowerShell 5.1. An optional release job boots the package on Windows and runs only `--version` and `--help`, and no automated check covers the native install. The install needs no administrator rights. WSL with the macOS, Linux and WSL command is the better-tested route.

```powershell
irm https://coder.iowarp.ai/install.ps1 | iex
```

PowerShell shows `PS C:\>` at the prompt. If `curl ... | sh` reports that `sh` is not recognized, you are in Windows rather than WSL.

### CMD

The same best-effort install, started from CMD.

```bat
powershell -NoProfile -Command "irm https://coder.iowarp.ai/install.ps1 | iex"
```

CMD shows `C:\>` without the `PS`. If you see `'irm' is not recognized as an internal or external command`, you ran the PowerShell command in CMD; use the command above.

### npm

With your own **Node.js 22.19 or newer** on `PATH`:

```sh
npm install -g @iowarp/clio-coder
```

### bun

```sh
bun add -g @iowarp/clio-coder
```

bun installs the package, but `clio-coder` still runs on Node.js, so it needs **Node.js 22.19 or newer** on `PATH` too.

## Confirm the installation

Open a new terminal and run:

```sh
clio-coder --version
```

It prints the installed version. If the shell says `clio-coder: command not found`, the launcher directory is not on your `PATH` yet. Add the line the installer printed to `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc`, or install again with `--modify-path`:

```sh
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
```

`command -v clio-coder` shows which file the name runs. If it is not `~/.local/bin/clio-coder`, an older install comes first on your `PATH`; remove it or reorder `PATH`. `clio-coder doctor` checks the installation and connections.

## Open a project

```sh
cd /path/to/your/project
clio-coder configure
clio-coder
```

On first launch, **Guided setup** asks what you have: an API key, a subscription, a model server or gateway, or a setup file from your lab or team. It sends the model one short test request and saves when the model answers. CLIO Coder has no account of its own; your provider may require credentials and charge for inference.

A new installation starts guided setup by itself, so `clio-coder configure` is optional. If you have used CLIO Coder before and no chat route is saved, it looks for a route it can use, such as a provider key in your environment, and opens chat with it. A model server found on a local port is used only after you say yes.

`/config` opens your connections inside a session, where **Add a target** runs setup again.

Prefer the desktop alpha? It is served from your own machine, opens in your browser, and shares the terminal's saved connections and settings. See [the desktop app](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/gui.html):

```sh
clio-coder gui --open
```

The browser has its own **Guided setup**; configuring in the terminal first is optional.

## Update, roll back and remove

Installer installs update themselves in the background, at most once a day. On Linux and macOS, npm, pnpm, bun, and volta installs whose prefix you own update after an interactive session quits and no other process of that install remains. Set `interface.autoUpdate: false` or `CLIO_CODER_AUTO_UPDATE=0` to keep only the notice. `/upgrade` reviews an update from inside the terminal. From the shell, update with the tool that installed it:

| Installed with | Update | Remove the program |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Installer | `clio-coder upgrade`. The new version installs beside the current one and must start before the launcher switches to it. | `clio-coder uninstall` |
| npm | `clio-coder upgrade` | `npm uninstall -g @iowarp/clio-coder` |
| bun | `bun add -g @iowarp/clio-coder@latest`, then `clio-coder upgrade --post-install` | `bun remove -g @iowarp/clio-coder` |

The installer keeps the previous version. `clio-coder upgrade --rollback` makes it current again. An install made with an exact `--version` stays pinned to that version until you run the installer with `--version latest`.

If an upgrade is refused over a setting the installed version cannot repair, the installer prints the new version's own `doctor --fix` command to run.

`clio-coder uninstall` removes your settings, credentials, sessions and caches, the launcher, the desktop app's background service, and for an installer install the managed Node and every package version. It previews what it will delete and asks first, and it stops with exit 1 while a session is open on this state directory. Add `--keep-binary` to keep the program, `--keep-config` to keep settings and credentials, or `--dry-run` to only look. Removing the program with npm or bun keeps those files. Project `.clio-coder/` directories are never removed.

If coder.iowarp.ai is unreachable, the latest GitHub release carries the full installer, at `https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/releases/latest/download/install.sh`.

## Give CLIO Coder a useful first task

Start with a request that lets you assess its understanding of your project:

> Explain how this repository builds and runs its tests. Identify the main entry points and suggest one verification task. Do not change files yet.

Then ask for a small change, name the files or behavior you care about, and tell CLIO Coder which checks should pass. Review the diff and recorded results before accepting the work.

Follow the [desktop and terminal walkthrough](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/desktop-and-terminal.html), or try [a numerical change with seven tests](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/temperature-calibration.html).

## Keep going

- [Connect a model](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html): setup, model selection, and saved settings.
- [Commands and shortcuts](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/commands-and-modes.html): the controls you'll use most.
- [Tools and permissions](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/tool-usage.html): understand changes and review checks.
- [Check your installation](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/doctor.html): diagnose a connection or setup problem.

## When you need more detail

These web guides cover the essentials. Detailed documentation ships with CLIO Coder; ask it to look up the bundled guide for the feature you're using. Each page also links to its full source guide.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/hpc-clusters.html

# Install on a cluster

Install CLIO Coder on a login node with an old glibc, a proxy, or no internet.

## Install without root

The installer brings its own Node.js, so you do not need `module load nodejs` or a system Node. It never uses `sudo` and refuses to run under it.

```sh
curl -fsSL https://coder.iowarp.ai/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
clio-coder doctor
```

It needs `curl` or `wget`, `tar` with `xz` or `gzip`, and a SHA-256 tool. The runtime and package go under `~/.local/share/clio-coder-install` and the launcher under `~/.local/bin`. Compute nodes that mount the same home directory run the same launcher.

## Work on the cluster

Ask for scheduler work in words, such as "submit job.sh and tell me when it starts". `sbatch`, `squeue` and the other Slurm, PBS, LSF and Flux clients run outside the sandbox with the same review as `ssh`: the safety judge decides first and asks you when it has no verdict, so name the action you want. Run them directly, not from a wrapper script, which stays inside the sandbox and fails.

Shell commands write to the project and temp folders without asking. Add scratch space with an absolute path:

```yaml
safety:
  scratchRoots: [/scratch/alice]
```

Keep results out of Git with `clio-coder store put results run-042.h5`; every checkout of the project on this host sees them.

## Old glibc, proxies, and quotas

The installer picks a Node build for the host. Official builds cover Linux with glibc 2.28 or newer, macOS, and Alpine on x64. An unofficial build covers x64 hosts with glibc 2.17 to 2.27, the RHEL and CentOS 7 class. Linux arm64 with an older glibc has no build; use conda-forge Node and npm instead.

Export `https_proxy` before running the installer behind a proxy. Node adds about 210 MB to a version, and the optional Claude Agent SDK is about 224 MB. The installer refuses to start with under about 732 MB free at the install root. On a small home quota, move the install root:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://coder.iowarp.ai/install.sh | sh -s -- --install-dir /project/$USER/clio-coder
```

## Verified downloads

Every Node download is checked against its release `SHASUMS256.txt`, and a mismatch stops the install. When `gpgv` or `gpg` is present, the installer also verifies the OpenPGP signature on official builds, and it stops when nodejs.org serves no signature or a key outside the Node.js release keyring signed it.

A mirror without a signature file still installs on the checksum. Set `CLIO_CODER_REQUIRE_SIGNATURE=1` to fail when no signature verifies.

## Airgapped sites and your own Node

Point `CLIO_CODER_NODE_MIRROR` at a mirror laid out like nodejs.org/dist, `CLIO_CODER_NODE_UNOFFICIAL_MIRROR` at one for the glibc 2.17 build, and `npm_config_registry` at a registry mirror for the package's dependencies. A Node mirror can be a `file://` URL on a shared filesystem.

If the site already provides Node 22.19 or newer, you can install with its npm instead: `npm install -g @iowarp/clio-coder`. When an older `node` comes first on `PATH`, set `CLIO_CODER_NODE` to the newer binary.

Pick versions with `--version` or `--channel`, and undo an upgrade with `--rollback`. The full guide covers the mirror variables; `sh install.sh --help` lists every option.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html

# Connect a model

Set up local models, institutional endpoints, and cloud connections.

## Connect the way you already work

Run `clio-coder configure`, or choose **Guided setup** in the desktop alpha. First-time setup asks what you have: an API key, a subscription, a model server or gateway, or a setup file from your lab or team. When CLIO Coder finds a route first, such as a provider key in your environment, it lists that route for you to choose.

1. Provide what the row asks for: paste a key, sign in to a subscription in the browser, or enter a server's address.
2. For a model server or gateway, CLIO Coder checks reachability and reads the model list.
3. CLIO Coder takes the provider's recommended model, or the only model a server lists. Otherwise you pick from the list. For a local server with no models, load one and choose **Check again**.
4. CLIO Coder sends the model one short test request and saves when it answers. After a failure you can try again, change the key or address, or choose **Save anyway**. The first connection supplies the chat and worker defaults.

The test request shows that the model answers. It does not establish model quality or tool calling, and `--no-verify` skips it. Live, cached, and provider-catalog model lists are labeled separately. Choose a model that supports tool calling for repository work.

Already know the URL? Use `clio-coder configure --quick` for endpoint-first setup. A lab or team can publish one setup file: `clio-coder configure --import <path-or-https-url>` reads it, prints where prompts will go, and asks once before saving.

## Use a local model server

Start LM Studio, Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, SGLang or Lemonade with a model that can call tools, then run `clio-coder`. It finds a server on its default port, such as Ollama on 11434, and offers it. On another address, run `clio-coder configure` and choose **A model server or gateway**. `clio-coder targets --probe --tools --target <id>` checks that the model really calls tools.

## Settings Center

Run `clio-coder configure --settings` or choose **Settings** on the desktop. Both use these sections:

| Section | What to change |
| --- | --- |
| Connections | Providers, credentials, endpoints, and model lists |
| Chat | The connection and model answering you |
| Fleet | Worker models, profiles, and capacity |
| Context & Memory | Context limits, compaction, and memory |
| Permissions & Limits | Approvals, autonomy, and spending limits |
| Appearance | Output style and interface preferences |
| Integrations | Agents, libraries, plugins, and Git |
| Advanced | Diagnostics and the full settings editor |

Terminal `/settings` groups the same controls into its own areas: Recent & Pinned, Models, Chat and display, Workers, Context and memory, Safety and limits, Workspace, and Advanced.

**Use connection default** lets a route inherit its connection's model. In the terminal, save to the session, project, or global scope where offered. Configure edits global defaults; desktop saved settings apply to new conversations. Active conversation controls have their own scope.

## Check the connection

```sh
clio-coder doctor
clio-coder targets --probe
```

If setup fails, check credentials, the endpoint address, and whether the local model is loaded. See [troubleshooting](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/troubleshooting.html) for the next step.

## Servers without a built-in runtime

Every connection names a runtime, which fixes how CLIO Coder talks to the server. `clio-coder configure --list` prints the runtime ids you can choose.

| Kind of server | Runtimes |
| --- | --- |
| Local model servers | `lmstudio`, `ollama`, `llamacpp`, `vllm`, `sglang`, `lemonade` |
| Cloud providers | `openai`, `anthropic`, `google`, `mistral`, `groq`, `deepseek`, `openrouter`, `bedrock`, and others |
| Any compatible endpoint | `openai-compat`, `anthropic-compat`, `litellm` |
| Another agent's login | `claude-code`, `codex-cli`, `opencode-cli`, `pi-cli`, and others; workers only |

A server that speaks the OpenAI or Anthropic API but has no runtime of its own usually works through `openai-compat` or `anthropic-compat`, or through a LiteLLM gateway. Local runtimes probe the server, report the loaded models, and price usage as free; the compatible runtimes make no local-server assumptions and never price as free.

When none of these fits, a developer can add a runtime as a plugin: a JavaScript file in the `runtimes/` folder of CLIO Coder's config directory, or an npm package listed under `integrations.runtimePlugins`, which takes effect after a restart. A broken plugin is reported on stderr and never stops startup. The [provider adapter cookbook](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/blob/beb9ea08bbde0994b8c14c17d6f2f97b9660c6cf/docs/architecture/provider-adapter-cookbook.md) describes the runtime descriptor a plugin exports.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/commands-and-modes.html

# Commands and shortcuts

Navigate the terminal, choose models, and control a session.

## Launch and inspect

| Command | Use it to |
| --- | --- |
| `clio-coder` | Open the terminal in your project |
| `clio-coder gui --open` | Open the local desktop alpha |
| `clio-coder configure` | Connect a model with Guided setup |
| `clio-coder doctor` | Check installation and connections |
| `clio-coder upgrade` | Update CLIO Coder |
| `clio-coder --help` | See installed commands |

For a single task without the interactive interface:

```sh
clio-coder run "Explain this project's test setup. Do not change files." --cwd /path/to/project
```

Add `--json` when you need machine-readable events. A request to avoid edits is task guidance; use the tool restrictions in the full guide when execution must be constrained.

## Everyday terminal commands

| Command | What it opens or does |
| --- | --- |
| `/help` | Commands and effective keybindings |
| `/model` | Model picker; apply to this session or save for the project or globally |
| `/settings` | Settings, grouped by area |
| `/config` | Connections in Settings; **Add a target** runs setup inside the session |
| `/library` | Skills, prompts, agents, playbooks, and plugins |
| `/context` | Context usage and pending handoffs |
| `/usage` | Session usage and supported subscription quotas |
| `/rewind` | Preview and restore this session's file snapshots |
| `/rename [name]` | Name the session so `/resume` can find it |
| `/fork [name]` | Fork from an assistant turn into a new session, optionally named |
| `/loop <interval> <task>` | Run a task as a fresh turn on a schedule while the session is idle |
| `/reload` | Reload settings, Library resources, and extension runtimes |
| `/restart` | Save the session and restart into it |
| `/resume` | Previous conversations; `/resume <id>` reopens one directly |
| `/tree` | Conversation history and branches |
| `/new` | A fresh conversation |
| `/view` | Artifacts and recorded results |
| `/trust` | Review the project's own CLIO Coder configuration and decide whether to activate it |
| `/poll <n> <question>` | Ask 2 to 5 independent agents the same question and see how they vote |
| `/report` | Draft a report for the maintainers; nothing is sent until you review it |

Familiar names work as aliases: `/clear` is `/new`, `/exit` is `/quit`, `/undo` is `/rewind`, `/cost` and `/status` open `/usage`, `/login` opens connections, and `/init` writes a project handbook. A mistyped command names the closest one and keeps your draft.

## A few keys to remember

Alt+letter runs a CLIO Coder action, and **Ctrl+G** then the same letter runs it in any terminal, including ones that intercept Alt. The menu also lists a few actions with no Alt key; arrows and Enter work too, and Esc closes it. On an empty composer, `?` shows the keys; `/help` shows every binding, custom ones included.

| Default key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Enter | Send; while running, queue the message for the next pause between tool calls |
| Ctrl+J | Insert a newline |
| Alt+S | Send now: interrupt the run and submit the draft |
| Alt+Q | Open the queue to reorder, edit, or remove waiting messages; `a` puts them all back in the draft |
| Alt+M | Open the model picker |
| Alt+L | Open the Library |
| Alt+O | Cycle the output detail level |
| Alt+W | Open Workers: the Fleet Runs board, or the workers dock in a session with panes |
| Alt+U | Open or close the one-page dashboard |

Ctrl+C closes an active overlay, cancels a running turn, or clears an idle draft. When idle with an empty draft and no queued messages, two presses within about 1.2 seconds exit.

For a course correction, type it in the composer and press **Alt+S** (or **Ctrl+G s**). Work already completed remains in the session record. In the queue, `t` moves a message to the end of the turn.

A clean exit prints a summary of the session and the `/resume <id>` line that reopens it. Sessions are resumed from inside the app, not with a command-line flag.

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/tool-usage.html

# Tools and permissions

Read, search, edit, and run commands with CLIO Coder's repository tools.

## Ask for a bounded change

CLIO Coder can read and search files, make edits, run shell commands, and execute declared project checks. Give it a concrete scope and an outcome you can review:

> Fix the parser's handling of empty input. Keep the public API unchanged, add the relevant regression test, and run the project's test check. Show the diff and result.

A useful sequence is **inspect → change → verify → review**. Inspect the actual diff before committing. The `git` tool can also run `add` and `commit`, and the safety rules judge those like the matching shell command.

## Understand permission requests

**default** follows one rule: containment first, judgment second, asking last. Workspace edits run. Shell commands run inside an OS sandbox when the host has one. In a Git work tree, CLIO Coder snapshots your files before the first change of a turn, and `/rewind` restores them. A safety judge reviews what would otherwise ask against your own messages, and you are asked when it has no verdict or the decision is yours.

**yolo** is for long jobs you leave running: nothing waits for you. It is contained by default, so the sandbox, snapshots, and safety judge work as at `default`, and a call that would have asked you is refused back to CLIO Coder. It needs a one-time acceptance. Set the level in Settings, with `--autonomy`, or with the leader key.

Unconfined yolo is the skip-permissions mode for a container or another disposable environment. Commands run unsandboxed as you, and only a short floor, your project rules, and the run's ceilings block. It takes effect only with `safety.yoloConfinement: unconfined` in your user settings and its own one-time acceptance. See [the containment tutorial](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/let-it-work-with-containment-and-rewind.html).

When a card reaches you, read the command and its working directory before approving it. A card nobody answers within `safety.unattendedAfterSeconds` (300 by default) is denied and the turn continues. In the terminal, a shell approval card also shows an **Effect** line that says in plain words what the command would do. It is a reading aid; admission does not depend on it.

Asking for a plan or saying “do not edit” guides the task; it does not establish a technical read-only boundary. Use the explicit tool restrictions or read-only dispatch options when you need that boundary.

## What the sandbox hides

A sandboxed command writes only to your project, the temp directories, your scratch roots, a private tool cache and the repository's Git data. It cannot read your SSH keys, cloud and code-host logins, registry tokens or the project's `.env` and key files, and credential variables are removed. A push or a publish needs those credentials, and a cluster scheduler command needs a host daemon the sandbox blocks, so each leaves the sandbox only once the safety judge or you allow it.

## Verify using your project's checks

Ask CLIO Coder to discover available checks, then run the relevant one with `verify`. It uses declared scripts and supported build/CI definitions rather than treating arbitrary output as a test result.

> Discover this project's verification checks. Run the test check through verify and report the exit status, failures, and anything you could not check.

On the desktop, the Session column's **Artifacts** card lists tool output and session records, and **Changes** lists the files a turn changed. In the terminal, use `/view` to browse artifacts and run records.

For checks that must accompany specific changes, add a [project quality policy](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/quality-policy.html). For a worked example, follow [the temperature-calibration tutorial](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/temperature-calibration.html).

## How tools reach the model

A main session starts with a small set of tools attached: `read`, `bash`, `edit`, `write`, `verify`, `ask_user`, and `gateway`, plus `dispatch` when workers are available and `consult` when a decision model is configured. The model finds every other capability through `gateway`, which can search the catalog, describe a tool's arguments, and call it. This keeps the request small while search, Git, web reading, data inspection, and MCP server tools stay one call away. Workers instead receive the tools their agent recipe admits.

Tool results are bounded. Each reading tool has a size cap per call, and all of them share a budget per turn that grows with the model's context window. A cut result ends with one notice line that says how much was shown and gives the exact argument for the next page. When the cap cut content that was already collected, the notice also names a read-only overflow copy in CLIO Coder's state directory, outside your workspace. The permission rules above apply to every tool, whether it is attached or reached through `gateway`.

## Limit what the agent may use

Run `clio-coder --allow-tools read,grep,find,ls` to limit the main agent to those tools, and `--delegate-tools` to limit its workers. Both take a comma-separated list or `none`. A prompt, skill or worker recipe can narrow these limits but never widen them. `/view` shows what the tools produced, a cut result in full included.

The full guide lists every tool and its limits. Developers can read [how the prompt and tool surface are assembled](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/blob/beb9ea08bbde0994b8c14c17d6f2f97b9660c6cf/docs/architecture/prompt-envelope-and-tools.md).

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/sandbox-and-safety.html

# Sandbox and safety

What a sandboxed command may do, what it hides, and when CLIO Coder asks you.

## Check your machine first

Run `clio-coder doctor` and read the `shell sandbox` row. `OK` means shell commands run inside an OS sandbox: bubblewrap on Linux and WSL, `sandbox-exec` on macOS (not yet verified on a real Mac). `WARN` means they run uncontained, so more of them ask first. Windows has no sandbox.

Then work at the `default` level. In your request, name anything that reaches beyond the project, such as "push the branch when the tests pass".

## What a sandboxed command may do

A sandboxed command can read your files and use the network. It writes only to the project, the temp directories, any directory in `safety.scratchRoots`, a private tool cache and the repository's Git data. Git hooks and Git config stay read-only, because they run later outside the sandbox.

## What the sandbox hides

The command cannot read SSH and GPG keys, the SSH agent, cloud and cluster logins, code-host and registry tokens, password stores, browser profiles, shell histories or other agents' logins. Secret files in the project, such as `.env` and `*.key`, are hidden too. Variables whose names or values look like credentials are removed. List one a build needs in `safety.sandboxPassEnv`.

## Commands that leave the sandbox

`git push`, `gh`, cloud CLIs, `ssh`, publishing commands and the Slurm, PBS, LSF and Flux clients need your credentials, so they run outside the sandbox. At `default` the safety judge reviews each one against your own messages first, and you are asked when it has no verdict. Contained yolo runs one only when your message names it.

## Stricter or looser

`safety.sandbox` is `auto` by default. `required` refuses workers' commands on a machine without a sandbox and keeps unconfined yolo sandboxed; `srun`, `salloc` and `flux` then stay inside it. `off` never sandboxes. Unconfined yolo, for containers only, runs commands as you with your credentials.

## Project configuration and /trust

A repository's own CLIO Coder settings, safety rules, hooks and packages are ignored until you approve their exact contents. A card lists them when you open the project, and `/trust` reopens it. Even approved, project settings can only make CLIO Coder more careful: they cannot raise the autonomy level, loosen the sandbox, raise limits or carry credentials.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/context-continuity.html

# Save and resume work

Resume conversations, manage context, and prepare a handoff.

## Pick up a conversation

In the terminal, use `/resume` to choose a previous session, or `/rename` first so you can resume it by name. On the desktop, open a saved conversation from **Overview** or **Sessions**. Saved history lets you continue with the context of earlier work.

Use `/tree` to inspect terminal conversation branches and `/fork [name]` to fork from an assistant turn into a new session, optionally named. `/tree` rewinds the conversation; `/rewind` restores files. On the desktop, open **Branches** in the Session column. Branches let you explore another direction while preserving the earlier conversation.

## Find sessions from the shell

`clio-coder session list` shows open sessions on this state directory, from any host that shares it, with host, pid, and last heartbeat. `clio-coder session terminate <id>` asks the owning process to exit.

## Keep long work focused

Open `/context` to inspect context usage, output reservation, remaining headroom, and any pending handoff. CLIO Coder compacts a long native session automatically when context use crosses its configured threshold, or you can request a focused summary:

```text
/context compact Keep the objective, decisions, changed files, test results, and remaining work.
```

For a fresh session with a stated goal, use `/handoff <goal>`. When moving work between agents, make sure the handoff includes evidence and unresolved questions, then review what the receiving agent does.

## Recover an interrupted handoff

If `/context` shows a pending handoff, use its exact ID:

```text
/context recover <handoffId> reduce
/context recover <handoffId> deliver
```

Choose `reduce` when the reduction has not committed and another attempt remains; choose `deliver` when a validated commit exists. If the continuation still cannot fit, compact more history first.

A restarted process records an interrupted handoff as paused and waits for your recovery command. A fork receives earlier notes as recall; it does not inherit permission to resume the parent's handoff.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/proactive-memory.html

# Memory and lessons

See what CLIO Coder remembers, approve lessons, or turn memory off.

## What memory does

Memory is on by default and needs no setup. CLIO Coder keeps task memory for a session: requirements, environment facts, failed attempts, and diagnoses. A rules tier runs without model calls. With no memory route of its own, the model tier uses your chat route within that route's cost, quota, or speed budget, so a default install spends some model calls on memory.

## See and approve lessons

Open `/memory` to see the lessons this session can reach, pending and rejected records beside approved ones, and what each one concerns. From the shell:

```sh
clio-coder memory list
clio-coder memory approve <memoryId>
clio-coder memory reject <memoryId>
clio-coder memory prune --stale
```

`/memory` also shows the current tier, the live bank, and the last twenty memory steps with their trigger, decision, and latency. That history is the only place a skipped step or a timeout appears. In `/memory`, press `p` on a selected row to propose it for review at repository scope, or `g` for global scope.

Memory also keeps commands a completed task proved to work, from its own run records, and offers them when a later session touches the same files. A repository lesson becomes standing guidance only after it is approved.

## Turn it off or route it elsewhere

Set `context.memory.enabled: false`, or use `/settings` → **Context and memory** → **Proactive memory**. Off means off: the `# Memory` section leaves main and worker prompts, and history review reads nothing from a session that ran with memory off. To run memory on its own route, set both `context.memory.target` and `context.memory.model`.

## Settings

All keys live under `context.memory` in `settings.yaml`. `/settings` has rows for `enabled`, the route, and `cadenceToolCalls`; set the others in the file.

| Key | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | `true` | Turns memory on or off. |
| `target`, `model` | `null` | Dedicated memory route; unset uses the chat route. |
| `cadenceToolCalls` | `10` | Minimum completed tools between background steps. |
| `trajectorySteps` | `8` | Recent tool steps a background step reads. |
| `maxOutputTokens` | `2000` | Bounds the bank context and the reminder. |
| `timeoutMs` | `60000` | Time limit for one background step. |

## Choose a cheap or local background model

Memory reads a short trajectory and writes a bounded result, so a small model usually suffices. CLIO Coder requests thinking off for this route.

```yaml
context:
  memory:
    target: memory-dedicated
    model: memory-profile/qwen3.5-4b
```

These IDs are examples; check yours with `clio-coder targets --probe`. Locally, both models and their caches must fit in memory.

## Cost and budget

A step is checked against its route's cost before any request leaves, so a skipped step costs nothing. Metered routes stop at `safety.limits.sessionCostUsd`, subscription routes wait out a near-full quota window, and free routes need an open request slot. Steps appear as `memory steps` in `/usage`.

Memory gives reminders; it does not replace reading the code or running the checks. See the full guide for how reminders are selected and when a lesson is promoted.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/panes-and-files.html

# Files and terminal panes

Attach files and open companion terminal panes.

## Add a file browser or companion shell

The terminal can open a files pane, a live workers dashboard, logs, a shell, music, or an installed coding peer beside the conversation.

Bare `clio-coder` in an interactive terminal opens its own private pane host with no question to answer. The host is a pinned copy of **Herdr** that the installer provisions. When it cannot start, CLIO Coder says so in one line and runs in the plain terminal.

After an npm or bun install, add the pane host yourself. The file browser is a separate install either way:

```sh
clio-coder panes install
clio-coder tools install yazi
```

To join a Herdr session of your own as a guest, open a pane in your project, then run:

```sh
clio-coder --with-panes
```

The option joins the current Herdr session. It does not create a pane host from a plain terminal. For the files pane, also enable it in your CLIO Coder settings:

```yaml
interface:
  panes:
    files:
      enabled: true
```

Check `clio-coder doctor` if the host or files engine is unavailable.

## Use the files pane

`/files` or **Alt+E** opens the file browser and gives it keyboard focus. Select a file and press **Ctrl+Y** to insert it as an `@file` mention and return focus to CLIO Coder. `/files` or Alt+E then hides the pane: the browser keeps running and keeps its directory. Press the key twice quickly, or run `/files close`, to end it.

## Docks hide instead of closing

The files, workers, and music panes are docks with fixed places. **Alt+E**, **Alt+W**, and **Alt+A** show or hide them, and a second press within a moment closes one. Alt+W opens a dashboard with a card for each worker in the session; Enter follows one worker's live stream.

`/music` plays focus radio through cliamp in a thin dock once `integrations.music.enabled` is on and `clio-coder tools install cliamp` has run. `/music pause`, `/music next`, `/music station <name or url>`, and `/music off` control it.

| Command | Companion pane |
| --- | --- |
| `/panes open shell` | A login shell in the workspace |
| `/panes open logs` | The newest dispatched run's event journal |
| `/panes show <run-or-agent>` | A live worker view |
| `/panes peer <agent> [brief]` | An interactive coding-agent handoff |

A session started inside tmux, Zellij, or screen stays in the plain terminal without panes. For editor and agent connections, see [interoperability](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/interop.html).

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/gui.html

# The desktop app

Open the desktop alpha, keep tasks in one window, and read the Session column.

## Open the desktop app

The desktop app is in alpha. It is a local web application: CLIO Coder serves it from your own machine on `127.0.0.1`, and it opens in your browser. It shares the terminal's saved connections and settings and covers a subset of terminal workflows.

```sh
clio-coder gui --open
```

Started this way, the app runs while that terminal stays open. On Linux with a systemd user session, including WSL, you can keep it running in the background instead. It then starts at login and appears in your app menu, or in the Windows Start Menu under WSL:

```sh
clio-coder gui background install --open
```

The installer offers the same step. The background app listens on port 4343, or 7373 when another program holds 4343. It uses saved credentials, so store a key that lives only in your shell with `clio-coder auth login <target>`.

`clio-coder gui` prints one link ending in `#ticket=`. The ticket opens one browser window once, within 60 seconds, and the browser then keeps its own short-lived sign-in. If a window shows the reconnect prompt, for example after the background app restarted, run `clio-coder gui` again or paste the new link into the prompt's **Launch link** field.

## One window, many tasks

Launching again brings the open CLIO Coder window forward under WSL, when the app is installed through Chrome or Edge, and on a Linux desktop with `wmctrl`, `xdotool` or sway when the background app is running. Otherwise it opens a new browser tab. Open a second window on purpose with **Open in new window** in a task's menu.

Any number of tasks can be open. Up to four turns run at once by default, and the `interface.guiTurnCapacity` setting allows 1 to 16. A further turn shows **Waiting for a slot** and starts when one frees. A task with no running turn that no window has shown for five minutes is paused. Its conversation stays readable, and **Resume session** continues it.

## Read the Session column

Beside each conversation, the Session column shows the workspace's path, branch and Git state, the model and its health, context, tokens and cost, the plan, artifacts, changed files, branches, agents, and evidence from run records. It updates as the task runs. **App activity** counts working, queued, and approval-waiting tasks across workspaces.

Type `/` in the composer for session commands such as `/context`, `/usage`, `/tree`, `/fork`, and `/handoff`.

## Approvals

With **Ask first**, reads, edits, and recognized commands run, and unrecognized shell commands, large dispatch plans, and anything that publishes outside the project wait on a card. The card states what the call is, what allowing it authorizes, and what it can affect. Choose **Allow once** or **Reject**.

**Run without asking** stops the cards for one task after a second confirmation. By default the sandbox, snapshots, and safety judge stay on, and a call that would have waited for you is refused back to CLIO Coder. It lasts until the task closes or is paused.

If a project carries settings, hooks, safety rules, extensions, or plugins you have not approved, the app lists the ignored files above the conversation with the command that reviews them.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/fleet-dispatch.html

# Workers and fleets

Assign focused tasks and combine workers into a workflow.

## Delegate a focused task

A worker handles a bounded task while CLIO Coder keeps the main conversation. Start with an explicit goal, files it may change, and the checks it should report.

```sh
clio-coder agents
clio-coder run "Inspect the parser's test coverage and report gaps. Do not edit files." --agent verifier
```

Use an agent ID from your installed catalog: `coder` makes changes, `tester` adds tests, and `debugger` and `verifier` only check. Add `--worktree` to `/run` to give an editing worker its own branch, or `--read-only` to make sure it changes nothing. A worker's answer stays out of the conversation until you run `/fleet share <runId>`, or start it with `--share`.

In the terminal, `/run <agent-id> <task>` starts a worker. The same command with a configured ACP peer's id, or `acp:<id>`, delegates to that peer. The **Workers** area of `/settings` chooses worker defaults without changing the chat model.

## Follow the work

Open **Workers** with Alt+W to inspect active runs. Select a running worker and use the displayed steer or cancel action. In a session with panes, Alt+W opens a live dashboard beside the conversation instead. You can also send an addressed message:

```text
@<agentId-or-runId-prefix> Focus on empty input and report the existing tests.
```

A steering message first reports queued, then received when the worker acknowledges it. Some external runtimes have no live steering channel; the interface identifies that limit. Review each run's recorded result before using its conclusions.

## Permissions, sandbox, and merges

Native workers run their shell, script, and verification commands in an OS sandbox: bubblewrap on Linux, or an experimental `sandbox-exec` profile on macOS. With the default `safety.sandbox: auto`, they run unsandboxed on a host with no sandbox backend; `required` refuses them instead, and `off` disables it. `safety.sandboxNetwork: true` allows network access.

Your own session's shell commands run in the same kind of sandbox at `default` and at contained `yolo`, which is yolo's default. At unconfined `yolo` they do not, and workers keep theirs. A worker's ordinary asks go to the safety judge by default (`fleet.permissions.mode: judge`).

When a worker's task branch would merge with a failing or unrun check, the terminal asks first with a **Merge task branch?** card showing the branch, changed paths, and the check. The card opens on **Keep branch**. Headless and ACP runs always keep the branch. `clio-coder fleet land` lists the branches finished runs kept, previews one, and lands it.

## Run a playbook when you need one

```sh
clio-coder playbook list
clio-coder fleet run sdlc --var task="Add empty-input handling to the parser"
clio-coder fleet status
```

A playbook combines workers into a workflow such as a review gate, competing solutions, or a council. The fleet runs it. Copy a builtin with `clio-coder playbook new <name> --from sdlc`, check it with `clio-coder playbook validate <name>`, and inspect the approval preview before starting. Its steps work and commit in your checkout, so there is nothing to land afterwards. See [the playbook tutorial](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/run-a-playbook-and-land-it.html).

## Give workers MCP tools

A recipe names exact `mcp_<id>__<tool>` capabilities, and admission refuses an untrusted or stale server. Check a server with `clio-coder mcp test <id>` and grant one project server with `clio-coder mcp trust <id>`. Add `--network` to allow it network inside the worker sandbox.

## Run workers on another machine

Remote native workers use SSH and need the same CLIO Coder version and the project at the same absolute path on each node. Add a node with `clio-coder fleet nodes add`, or in the terminal under `/settings fleet`, which opens the Workers area.

A node receives work only after `clio-coder fleet nodes test <id> --record` passes for this project; the record lasts one day. Adding a node moves nothing by itself: unpinned work stays local.

Start locally with one worker. Use the full guide for remote-node configuration, capacity, recipes, and failure recovery.

## When a worker stops or fails

A worker has no operator watching it, so `fleet.permissions.mode` decides what happens when it needs an approval. The default, `judge`, sends a local worker's ordinary request to the main session's safety judge while that session runs at `default`; elsewhere it denies. A refused shell command goes back to the worker as a tool result, and the third refusal ends the run with exit 3 and outcome `permission_required`. The reason names every refused command. Under `fail`, the first refusal ends the run.

Some failures retry automatically and some never do:

- A provider 429 retries on another target after at least one second; a 401 or 403 also moves to another target, and a 408 retries.
- Other provider 4xx errors, cancellation, policy and permission refusals, and deterministic outcomes such as `worker_no_work` never retry.
- No attempt retries automatically after it ran a state-changing call, or when its records cannot prove the checkout unchanged.
- Backoff starts at 500 ms, doubles, and stops at 60 seconds.

A remote node that fails its channel twice in a row is marked offline. Its in-flight runs settle as `stalled` and retry without that node, and each reroute is recorded on the run. Read the stop reason in **Workers** or with `clio-coder fleet status` before retrying by hand. The [dispatch mechanics reference](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/blob/beb9ea08bbde0994b8c14c17d6f2f97b9660c6cf/docs/architecture/worker-dispatch-mechanics.md) gives the full failure taxonomy and exit codes.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/resource-library.html

# Skills and resources

Browse and use skills, prompts, agents, fleets, and plugins.

## Find a useful skill

The Library contains **skills, agents, prompts, playbooks, plugins, and extensions**. Open `/library` or press **Alt+L**. Switch categories with left/right, search with `/`, and open a package with Enter.

`clio-coder library update --all` updates eligible copies, `clio-coder library package <directory>` turns a skill directory into a package, and `clio-coder library validate` checks what you author.

Use **Browse** to find available content and **Installed** to manage your copies. Choose **User** for tools shared across projects or **Project** for resources specific to this workspace.

`install` uses user scope unless you pass `--project`; `s` switches scope in the Library. Project packages live under `.clio-coder/plugins/`.

For example, preview and install the test-driven-development skill:

```sh
clio-coder library install skill:tdd --project --dry-run
clio-coder library install skill:tdd --project
```

Then activate it in the terminal:

```text
/skill tdd Add coverage for this parser before changing its behavior.
```

## Write your own prompts and skills

A file such as `.clio-coder/prompts/bugfix.md` runs as `/bugfix`. A `SKILL.md` with a `description` in `.clio-coder/skills/<name>/` loads with `/skill <name>`. Prompts and skills that Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode keep in your home folder are found without copying; copies inside a project wait until you trust them.

Move your prompts, skills and settings to another machine with a share archive:

```sh
clio-coder share export --out project.clio-coder-share.json --project
clio-coder share import project.clio-coder-share.json --dry-run
```

## Command reference

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `library search [query] [--kind <kind>]` | Find packages in the index |
| `library list` | Show packages in both scopes |
| `library install <ref> [--dry-run]` | Review and install a package |
| `library update <ref>\|--all` | Bring installed copies forward |
| `library enable`, `disable`, `remove <ref>` | Change one installed copy |

Prefix each with `clio-coder`. A reference is `kind:name`, such as `skill:tdd`, or an unambiguous bare name. `update --all` skips extensions, which each need their own review.

## Review before installing

The install review shows the destination, dependencies, and verified package pin. In the Library, the selected row offers install, update, enable/disable, and remove actions when applicable. Management actions name the owning package and selected scope.

Project packages take precedence over matching user packages. A disabled project copy also suppresses the user copy, so a project can explicitly keep a resource unavailable. A project package set you have not approved for the workspace is listed but not loaded, and does not override your user copy; see [plugins](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/plugins.html).

## Trust project packages

A project copy comes from the repository, so its digest proves integrity, not your consent. Approve project packages per workspace:

```sh
clio-coder config trust plugins
clio-coder config trust plugins --hash <sha256>
```

The first is a read-only review; the second approves what you reviewed, and `--revoke` withdraws it. `/reload library` applies it to a running session. A changed package identity needs a new review, and an import never approves one.

## Refresh a running session

After changing recipes through another process, run:

```text
/reload library
```

Disabling a package prevents subsequent discovery; it does not stop an in-flight tool or erase instructions already read. Disable deletes no files; `library enable <ref>` restores the package. Disabling and removal apply without a reload, while installs from another process need `/reload library`. `/skill off` clears an active skill's armed tool surface without erasing earlier context.

For bundles of related resources, see [plugins](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/plugins.html). To review resources from other coding agents, see [interoperability](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/interop.html).

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/plugins.html

# Install plugins

Add reusable resources to your CLIO Coder installation.

## Install a bundle of resources

Plugins keep related skills, prompts, agents, playbooks, and supporting files together. Browse the shipped catalog and preview an installation before writing it:

```sh
clio-coder library list --kind plugin
clio-coder library install plugin:materio --dry-run
clio-coder library install plugin:materio
```

The catalog ships with CLIO Coder, but its content is not installed automatically. Add `--project` to keep a package in the current workspace; otherwise installation uses user scope.

Project packages load only in a workspace you have approved. Your own first project install approves it. After that, a change to the project's package set, including one that arrives with a clone or a pull, stays listed but unloaded until you review it with `clio-coder config trust plugins` and run the approval command it prints.

A local bundle uses the same review flow:

```sh
clio-coder library install ./my-plugin --project
```

## Keep the installed copy under control

```sh
clio-coder library inspect materio --json
clio-coder library drift materio
clio-coder library disable materio
clio-coder library enable materio
```

Installation records a verified pin covering the complete package tree. Drifted content is blocked from loading; `pin` verifies the recorded pin rather than approving edits. Review an update before replacing a modified copy.

In the terminal, open **Library → Plugins** to browse members and review lifecycle actions. Run `/reload library` after changing recipes externally.

## Choose the right kind of extension

A plugin carries content. An extension is code that runs in its own process, declares everything it may do, and loads only after you approve those capabilities; manage it with `clio-coder extensions`. The runtime is sandboxed where the host has a backend. Project extensions also need `clio-coder config trust extensions`. See [the extension tutorial](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/write-an-extension-with-declared-capabilities.html). Adding tool schemas requires a new session; recipe reload does not change those schemas.

See [skills and resources](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/resource-library.html) for everyday Library controls. The full plugin guide covers private catalogs and package authoring.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/harness-extensions.html

# Write and install extensions

Install and write extensions that declare what they may do.

## Plugin or extension

A plugin carries content such as skills, prompts, and playbooks. An extension is code that runs in its own process, declares everything it may do, and loads only after you approve those capabilities.

## Manage extensions

```sh
clio-coder extensions list
clio-coder extensions install <path>
clio-coder extensions disable <id>
clio-coder extensions remove <id>
```

`install` prints what the package would be allowed to do and records the digest of that declaration. If the manifest changes between review and apply, the install refuses and asks for a fresh review. In a session, `/extensions` shows each package's state, commands, and confinement.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `init <id> [--template <name>]` | Scaffold a manifest, entrypoint, and test |
| `validate <path>` | Check the manifest; print the envelope and its digest |
| `install <path> [--user\|--project]` | Review and install; user scope by default |
| `enable`, `disable`, `remove <id>` | Change one installed copy |
| `run <id> <command>` | Run one extension command headlessly |

Prefix each with `clio-coder extensions`. `enable`, `disable`, and `remove` act on the project copy when one exists, unless `--user` or `--project` selects one.

## Where packages live

User packages live under `<configDir>/extensions/<id>/`, project packages under `.clio-coder/extensions/<id>/`. A project package shadows the user package with the same ID, even when disabled, but only once you approve project extensions for the workspace:

```sh
clio-coder config trust extensions
clio-coder config trust extensions --hash <sha256>
```

The first is a read-only review; the second approves it. Until then a project copy lists as `untrusted` and the user copy keeps loading.

## What an extension can add

Hooks at prompt submit and around tool calls, runtime tools the model can call, status lines, panels, and work on a timer. A `before_tool` hook can refuse a call. The runtime runs inside bubblewrap on Linux or Seatbelt on macOS when a backend exists; without one, it runs with your permissions.

Approval covers the manifest's `runtime` block, the capability envelope: commands, hooks, tools with their action class, interface slots, content the runtime may see (`prompt`, `tool-args`, `tool-results`, `assistant-text`), file roots, and whether it may run programs or use the network.

Command tools under `capabilities.tools` run a `node` or `python3` script per call. The command runs inside your session's OS sandbox when admission contains the call, as it contains `bash` at `default`; otherwise it runs with your access. Prefer a runtime tool when confinement matters.

## Write one

```sh
clio-coder extensions init <id> --template status
```

The templates are `status`, `hook`, `panel`, `tool`, and `workspace`. Follow [the extension tutorial](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/write-an-extension-with-declared-capabilities.html) for the whole path. A project's own extensions also need `clio-coder config trust extensions`.

The manifest, `clio-coder-extension.yaml`, requires `id`, `version`, and `description`:

```yaml
id: lab-guard
version: 1.0.0
description: Refuse writes to protected paths.
runtime:
  api: 2
  entrypoint: runtime/extension.ts
  commands:
    - { name: protect, description: Protect a path against write and edit calls. }
```

The code must register exactly what the manifest declares, and CLIO Coder never installs dependencies. Run `validate` and `test`, then `install`; a running session picks it up after `/reload extensions`.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/interop.html

# Editors and other agents

Use supported agent connections and editor integrations.

## Bring an installed coding agent

CLIO Coder can dispatch a focused task to a configured coding peer or open an interactive handoff pane. Install and authenticate that peer's own CLI first, then inspect what is available:

```sh
clio-coder interop inspect --json
clio-coder configure --interop
```

In the terminal, `/library interop` shows available connections. Supported managed modes vary by peer: Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode have ACP recipes; other peers may use a headless CLI or a pane.

- `/run <agent-id> <task>` uses a configured ACP connection; `/run acp:<id> <task>` names one explicitly.
- `/run --target <target> <agent> <task>` uses a configured headless target.
- `/panes peer [--cwd <path>] <agent> [brief]` opens an interactive pane beside the conversation.

Managed ACP and headless runs record results in sealed run records. A pane is an interactive handoff and does not produce a run record. For a headless task, `--worktree` preserves a Git task branch for review; it does not confine the peer's filesystem or network access.

A peer that runs its own tool loop is refused write-capable work unless you trust it with `trustedUnmediated: true` in your user settings: on the target for a headless peer, or on its external-agent entry for an ACP peer.

## Review resources from another agent

The Library can discover supported foreign resources and review their origin, scope, trust, and actual availability before adoption. It identifies unsupported components rather than treating an entire foreign package as compatible.

Open `/library`, then use its local-agent discovery action. Inspect the proposed resources and approve the ones you want in your user or project library.

## Connect an ACP frontend

To use CLIO Coder from an editor that speaks the Agent Client Protocol (ACP), point the editor's ACP agent entry at `clio-coder acp`. The editor then exchanges JSON-RPC with that process over stdio, with session listing, resume, modes, and model options.

```sh
clio-coder acp --cwd /path/to/project
```

`clio-coder --acp` is an exact alias. These launch options are the operator's limits; a client can narrow them but never widen them:

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--cwd PATH` | Pins the workspace. Without it, the editor's first session request selects it. |
| `--permission-timeout MS` | Longest wait, in milliseconds, for one permission answer from the editor; 120000 by default. |
| `--allow-tools NAMES` | Limits the session's tools to these comma-separated names, as `clio-coder run` does; `none` disables all. |
| `--delegate-tools NAMES` | Limits the tools the session's dispatched workers may hold. |
| `--read-only` | Holds every session at the read-only ceiling. No file outside CLIO Coder's own home changes. |

`clio-coder acp auth login` opens the interactive Quick Connect setup, so an editor's terminal sign-in step can create a connection. Stdout carries only protocol messages; diagnostics go to stderr. The [ACP protocol reference](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/blob/beb9ea08bbde0994b8c14c17d6f2f97b9660c6cf/docs/architecture/acp.md) covers capabilities, authentication, permissions, and telemetry in detail. Consult the full guide for peer-specific setup and for installing CLIO Coder's portable library in other agents.

## Built on the Pi SDK

CLIO Coder's model connections, agent loop, and terminal interface are built on the Pi SDK. Version 0.8.0 pins the Pi 1.5.2 packages to exact versions and bundles the one terminal package it patches, so an npm install needs no patch step. CLIO Coder owns everything above that layer: permissions, workers, sessions, run records, and its own handling for local model servers.

Pi's coding agent is also a delegation peer. With the `pi` command installed and signed in, a target on the `pi-cli` runtime runs headless worker tasks under Pi's own login. Like other peers that run their own tool loop, it needs `trustedUnmediated: true` on the target before it may take write-capable work. Developers upgrading the SDK can read the [Pi SDK boundary](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/blob/beb9ea08bbde0994b8c14c17d6f2f97b9660c6cf/docs/architecture/pi-boundary.md).

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/slurm.html

# Slurm workflows

Connect CLIO Coder to supported Slurm tools for cluster work.

## Work with a scheduler

CLIO Coder connects to Slurm through the stdio MCP server shipped by [clio-kit](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-kit). The server provides job submission, listing, description, cancellation, and cluster information. A working scheduler connection is required; client binaries alone are not enough.

## Set up the server

Install clio-kit (for example `uv tool install clio-kit`) on a host where `sbatch`, `squeue`, `scontrol`, and `scancel` reach your cluster. Declare the server in `mcp.yaml` in your config directory, which `clio-coder paths` prints:

```yaml
version: 1
servers:
  - id: slurm
    command: clio-kit
    args: [mcp-server, slurm]
    timeoutMs: 120000
```

Keep the id `slurm`; the skill and the approval rules below expect it. Run `clio-kit mcp-server slurm` once in a terminal and stop it with Ctrl-C, because a cold first launch can exceed the 15 second initialize bound. A project declaration in `.clio-coder/mcp.yaml` needs `clio-coder mcp trust slurm` first.

## Check with doctor

`clio-coder doctor --verbose` prints one Slurm row when nothing is set up and three once anything is, none of which fails doctor.

| Row | What it reports |
| --- | --- |
| `slurm clio-kit` | `clio-kit` on `PATH` and whether it lists `slurm` |
| `slurm mcp server` | Which `mcp.yaml` declares it, its scope, and its trust |
| `slurm scheduler` | Whether `sbatch` and `squeue` answer `--version` |

An OK scheduler row does not prove a working scheduler; it never contacts the controller.

## Use a job workflow

Install the project-scoped Slurm skill:

```sh
clio-coder library install skill:slurm-jobs --project
```

Then ask it to run a specific script and report the evidence:

```text
/skill slurm-jobs Submit this script, wait for its terminal state, and report the job ID, exit code, stdout, and stderr paths.
```

The skill submits once, polls through the MCP server, and reports the outcome. It does not fall back to shell `sbatch` when the server is unavailable.

## Choose approvals deliberately

With the server declared as `slurm`, CLIO Coder classifies the `mcp_slurm__` tools by name:

| Capability | Class | At `default` | At `yolo` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `slurm_list`, `slurm_describe`, `slurm_cluster` | `read` | Runs | Runs |
| `slurm_submit`, `slurm_cancel` | `execute` | Safety judge reviews; you decide when it has no verdict | Contained, the default: the judge reviews, and a call with no verdict is refused. Unconfined: runs |

In a headless `clio-coder run` at `default`, a submission or cancellation runs only when the safety judge allows it.

A `toolActionClasses` entry in `mcp.yaml` can reclassify one tool, but submission and cancellation keep their confirmation at `default`. Review the full guide before changing a classification or enabling unattended execution. For small local changes, begin with [ordinary project checks](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/tool-usage.html).

## Run a parameter sweep

The `hpc-sweep` skill in the `hpc` plugin runs a sweep as one job array:

```sh
clio-coder library install plugin:hpc --project
```

Run `/reload library`, then `/skill hpc-sweep dry run sweeps/decay.yaml`. The sweep file names `parameters`, a `mode` (`grid` or `sample`), a run `template`, `resources`, a `concurrency` cap, and a verify `check`. The skill submits only on your word, checks each run, and writes verdicts to `sweeps/<name>/results.md`.

For this release, this path was checked against fake Slurm clients only, not a live controller.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/doctor.html

# Check your installation

Diagnose installation and connection problems with doctor.

## Start with the standard check

Run doctor from your project:

```sh
clio-coder doctor
```

It checks the installation, configured connections, model-list evidence, local worker capacity, and relevant tools. Standard doctor is read-only, uses passive probes, and sends no model generation request. In the terminal, `/doctor` shows the findings in your session.

Read three rows first: `chat` names your route and what is missing, each `connection <id>` row says whether the key is there and the endpoint answered, and `shell sandbox` says whether commands run in an OS sandbox. Fix `!!` rows first; a `WARN` row still lets CLIO Coder work.

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--verbose` | Print every row instead of folding quiet families |
| `--json` | Emit findings as JSON on stdout |
| `--deep` | Add the live tool probe and validation dry run |
| `--tools-timeout <seconds>` | Bound each tool probe; default 120, needs `--deep` |

Doctor exits 0 when no row is an error, 1 when one is, and 2 on a usage error.

## Read the findings

| Badge | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| OK | The check passed |
| INFO | A fact that usually needs no action, such as an HPC compiler that is not on `PATH` |
| WARN | Worth attention; CLIO Coder can still work |
| !! | A broken requirement; doctor exits with an error |

A live model list, a cached list, and a provider catalog are distinct evidence. A reachable endpoint does not establish that a model will answer well or call tools. The capacity row reports CPUs and available memory; it does not measure GPU memory or model fit.

## Common rows and their fix

The first row, `chat`, says whether chat can run and what to run when it cannot.

| Row | Usual cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `settings.yaml` | Invalid keys, named in the row | Edit those keys |
| `credentials` | `credentials.yaml` is missing or not `0600` | `clio-coder doctor --fix` |
| `lifecycle migrations` | Migrations are pending after an update | `clio-coder upgrade` |
| `connection <id>` | Missing credential or no endpoint answer | Check the target and sign-in |
| `model <id>` | The role model is missing from a live list | Pick a listed model |
| `external tool <id>` | A pinned helper is missing | `clio-coder tools install <id>` |

## HPC toolchain rows

`toolchain <name>` rows cover compilers, MPI, `nvcc`, build tools, `python3`, and `sbatch`. An absent tool is `INFO`. It is `WARN` when your validation contract's validators need it, or when a tool's `--version` fails, as with an unconfigured Slurm client.

## Repair or investigate further

`clio-coder doctor --fix` creates missing directories and template files, makes `settings.yaml` and `credentials.yaml` owner-only, rewrites retired setting values such as `safety.autonomy: auto-edit` and YAML `on` and `off` booleans while keeping your comments, and records fleet preflight results. Plain `doctor` previews the settings rewrite. Version migrations still run through `clio-coder upgrade`.

The `shell sandbox` row says whether this host contains your commands and where they may write.

For a live tool-use probe and validation-contract dry run:

```sh
clio-coder doctor --deep
```

Deep checks send model requests and may consume tokens. Allow more time for a cold local model with `--tools-timeout <seconds>`. Use `--json` for structured findings.

A `tools <target>` row is `OK` when the model streamed a valid tool call and `WARN` when the call was malformed or the target did not answer. A `validator <n>` row says whether each validator command would run without an approval ask; nothing is executed. In a session, use `/doctor --deep`.

If a connection remains unavailable, follow [troubleshooting](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/troubleshooting.html).

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/troubleshooting.html

# Troubleshooting

Resolve common connection, terminal, and runtime problems.

## First problems

| You see | Do this |
| --- | --- |
| `clio-coder: command not found` after installing | Open a new shell, or run the `export PATH=...` line the installer printed last. |
| `<target> at <url> did not answer (...)` | Start the model server, or change the address with `/config`. |
| `<provider> has no key or sign-in stored.` or HTTP 401 | Run the `clio-coder auth login` command it names, or fix the key in `/config`. |
| `... reports no tool support` | Pick a model that calls tools with `/model`. |
| `shell sandbox` is `WARN` in doctor | On Linux, install `bubblewrap`. CLIO Coder still works; more commands ask first. |
| A call was denied because nobody answered | Name the action in your request, or set `safety.unattendedAfterSeconds: 0` to wait for you. |

## A connection is unavailable

Start with these diagnostics:

```sh
clio-coder doctor
clio-coder targets --probe
```

Check that the selected endpoint is reachable, required credentials are present, and the model is loaded. A local server with an empty model list usually needs a model loaded before setup can finish. In **Connections**, reopen Guided setup or repair the saved connection.

For slow first responses from a local model, check the server's load state and capacity. Live tool-use behavior can be investigated with `clio-coder doctor --deep`; it makes generation requests.

## Settings fail to load

CLIO Coder uses a strict version-2 settings schema. Invalid or retired keys produce a diagnostic naming the path. `clio-coder upgrade` applies the registered migration and preserves the original version-1 settings as a backup. Plain `clio-coder doctor` previews the fix for a retired value, and `doctor --fix` applies it.

Use [Configuration essentials](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/configuration-reference.html) to find the settings layers and the full reference.

## A terminal shortcut does not arrive

Open **Ctrl+G** and choose the corresponding menu action. A terminal or multiplexer may intercept Alt shortcuts. **Ctrl+J** is the portable newline; `/help` shows your effective bindings.

If a files or companion pane is unavailable, run `clio-coder doctor` and read its `panes` and `external tool` rows. `clio-coder panes install` adds a missing pane host, and `clio-coder tools install yazi` adds the file browser. See [files and terminal panes](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/panes-and-files.html).

## Work stopped or a check failed

Read the recorded command and output in the desktop's **Artifacts** card or terminal `/view`. A failed test can point to a useful next task; ask CLIO Coder to explain the failure before changing the test's acceptance criteria.

For an interrupted context handoff, inspect `/context` and follow [save and resume work](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/context-continuity.html).

## Report a problem to the maintainers

`/report` in the terminal and `clio-coder report` in a shell draft a bug report, a feature request or a question. `--last` adds what CLIO Coder observed in the newest session in this folder.

```sh
clio-coder report bug --title "footer flickers on resize" --last --dry-run
```

You review the draft exactly as it will be posted. Local paths, user, host, project and branch names, e-mail and IP addresses, and secrets are masked first, and a draft that still holds this machine's names is refused. Nothing is sent until you press `s` in the terminal, answer the prompt in a shell, or pass `--yes`. `--dry-run` stops after the preview.

With a signed-in `gh`, CLIO Coder searches GitHub for the same problem, then posts a public issue or discussion under your account. Without `gh` it opens a prefilled form in the browser. A diagnostic bundle is opt-in, encrypted for the maintainers, and shared only from your own shell. CLIO Coder never sends anything on its own.

## Exit codes

Every `clio-coder` command uses the same exit codes, so a script can tell why a run stopped:

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | Success, including `--help`, `--version`, and a `--dry-run`. |
| `1` | Operational failure: an unreachable model, unresolved doctor findings, or a worker whose changes were withheld or who did no work. |
| `2` | Usage error: an unknown command, flag, target, or agent, or a global flag placed after the subcommand. |
| `3` | A dispatched worker was stopped by its permission refusal limit (`permission_required`). |
| `4` | The priced spend ceiling was reached: `safety.limits.sessionCostUsd` (5 USD by default) or `run --max-cost-usd`. |
| `75` | An install or upgrade is busy; nothing changed, so retry later. |
| `124` | `clio-coder run --timeout` elapsed. |
| `141` | The reader of a `clio-coder run` stdout closed, as in `clio-coder run ... \| head -1`. |
| `129`, `130`, `143` | Stopped by SIGHUP, SIGINT, or SIGTERM. |

A few commands, such as `fleet events`, `telemetry verify`, `research start`, and `arena run`, give small codes their own meaning; the full guide lists them. In a headless `clio-coder run`, the answer or JSON stream goes to stdout, while progress and diagnostics go to stderr. [Automate with clio-coder run](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/exit-codes-and-output.html) has the details.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/quality-policy.html

# Require project checks

Choose the declared checks a change requires and inspect verification freshness.

## Tell CLIO Coder what “checked” means in your project

A quality policy names the declared checks required when particular files change. Your repository supplies the standards; CLIO Coder records verification and assesses whether the results still match the current inputs.

At a Git workspace root, create `.clio-coder/quality.yaml`:

```yaml
version: 1
rules:
  - id: source
    paths: ["src/**", "tests/**"]
    inputs: ["src/**", "tests/**", "package.json", "package-lock.json"]
    checks: [test]
    allowLimitations: false
```

This example assumes the root `package.json` declares a `test` script. Adapt the paths, lockfile, and check IDs to your project. Include configuration, fixtures, and helper files that affect the result. CLIO Coder does not create or modify this policy automatically.

## Run the declared checks

Ask CLIO Coder to discover verification checks, then run each required ID through `verify` without argument or working-directory overrides. For a subproject, declare a root script or a verifier-catalog entry with its working directory.

The policy names existing checks; it cannot introduce shell commands or bypass approval. A narrowed test run or an unrelated passing command cannot satisfy a required full check.

## Review freshness

CLIO Coder compares source, check-declaration, and policy fingerprints. Edits after a passing run can make the result **stale**; a later failing run supersedes an earlier pass. Missing or unavailable evidence remains unverified.

A valid policy selects high rigor by default, which requests continuation for outstanding checks when recovery is possible. Setting `CLIO_CODER_RIGOR=normal` makes the assessment advisory. Neither mode grants additional execution authority.

Snapshots need Git and a workspace at the repository root. They cover tracked and nonignored untracked source, not external datasets, installed dependencies, or running services. Use domain-specific checks for those requirements. The full guide explains bounded snapshots and permitted limitations.

Try [the calibration example](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/temperature-calibration.html) to see a declared check and its actual result.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/research-and-arena.html

# Climb a metric, compare models

Improve a measured number with verified research campaigns, and compare models blind in the arena.

## Improve a number, and keep only real gains

`clio-coder research start` runs CLIO Coder's agent repeatedly to move one measured number in your project, such as the wall time of a benchmark. The number is a key in the JSON that a check in `.clio-coder/verifiers.yaml` prints. Correctness checks run as gates.

```yaml
version: 2
checks:
  - id: bench
    description: Wall time of stats.py on 3000 values (min is better)
    kind: command
    command: [python3, bench.py]   # prints {"wall_ms": 12.3}
    cwd: .
    timeoutMs: 60000
    tags: [benchmark]
  - id: correct
    description: stats.py answers match the reference on a holdout input
    kind: numeric-compare
    command: [python3, check.py]
    reference: tests/reference/stats.json
    tolerance: { relative: 1.0e-9 }
    cwd: .
    timeoutMs: 60000
    tags: [correctness]
```

Commit this file so every research worktree contains it.

```bash
clio-coder research start --check bench --metric wall_ms --direction min \
  --max-iterations 5 --gate correct --scope stats.py --max-wall-minutes 30
```

Each attempt runs in its own Git worktree. Before the first attempt, an A/A check of the base against itself refuses a noisy measurement unless `--allow-noisy`. A change is kept only when it clears both measurement tests and every gate passes:

- **Measurement:** across interleaved trials, the median improves by at least 5% and a seeded bootstrap interval excludes zero.
- **Gates:** every gate check passes in the change's worktree.

Kept changes go to the branch `clio/research/<id>`; your own branch is never touched. Unknown spend never counts as zero. `clio-coder research report <id>` regrades every verdict from the stored samples.

## Budgets and stopping

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--max-iterations <N>` | Required hard stop on iterations |
| `--max-wall-minutes <M>` | Deadline that also ends the step in flight |
| `--max-cost-usd <X>` | Spend cap; an unpriced run stops the campaign unless you pass `--allow-unpriced` |
| `--min-improvement <frac>` | Relative gain to clear; default 0.05 |
| `--trials <N>` | Interleaved base and candidate pairs; default 5 |

## Where results go

Campaigns live in `.clio-coder/research/<id>/` and arena matches in `.clio-coder/arena/<match-id>/`. Check progress with `clio-coder research status` or `research list`.

| Exit code | `research start` |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | A budget cap ended the campaign |
| 1 | An error, a noisy A/A check, or unenforceable spend |
| 2 | Usage error |
| 130, 143, 129 | Stopped by Ctrl-C, SIGTERM, or SIGHUP |

## Compare models blind

`clio-coder arena run` gives one prompt to 2 to 4 target/model pairs, each in its own worktree. `arena show` hides which model produced which answer until you vote with `arena vote`. `arena standings` counts the votes and adds an Elo rating once a model has 5 votes. CLIO Coder never grades a contender. The desktop app's Arena page runs the same commands.

```sh
clio-coder arena run --check unit \
```
