```sh
  --contender copilot/claude-haiku-5.5 --contender litellm/mini/qwen3.8-27b-iq4r-v4 \
  -- "Fix the bug in calc.py so test_calc.py passes."
clio-coder arena show <match-id>
clio-coder arena vote <match-id> A --note "smaller diff"
clio-coder arena show <match-id> --reveal
```

Before a vote, `show` hides each target, model, cost, and duration, and `--reveal` is refused. Vote with a label, `tie`, or `both-bad`; `--replace` changes your vote.

Research and the arena are new in 0.7.0. With `--autonomy yolo` both run contained yolo: the sandbox, the safety judge, and your autonomous caps stay on, and unconfined yolo is refused. `clio-coder research resume <id>` continues a stopped campaign from its journal with the same spec and budget.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/store.html

# Keep results in the store

Keep datasets and results outside the working tree, with a record of where each came from.

## Keep results out of your working tree

Long analyses produce files you want to keep but not commit: datasets, model outputs, figures. The project store holds them outside the working tree. The main session, its workers and every linked worktree of the project see the same store, and each file keeps a record of where it came from.

A tag is a named container, classed input, output, cache or archive. A blob is a file in a tag. A reference reads `<tag>:<blob>`, such as `results:summary.parquet`.

## Store a file from your shell

```sh
clio-coder store put results out/summary.parquet --note "baseline run"
clio-coder store tags
clio-coder store ls results
clio-coder store stat results:summary.parquet
```

`put` creates a missing tag as an input tag. `stat` shows the record and whether the bytes have drifted since: `none`, `changed`, `missing` or `unrecorded`. `get` prints the path of a read-only copy, or copies the blob elsewhere with `--to <path>`. Every command takes `--json`.

## Ask CLIO Coder to use it

> Run the analysis script on `data:measurements.h5`, put its summary into the `results` tag, and tell me whether the stored baseline has drifted.

The agent reaches the store through its `store` tool. Reads run without asking. Creating a tag, a put and a note are judged as writes. Removing a blob, or a put that replaces one, asks first and names the blob; a replacing put also states its size. The store keeps no earlier versions.

When a `run_script` run declares a store blob as an input and its output is put back, the record names the script and that input.

## Let workers write

Dispatched workers read the store. They write only into the tags their dispatch grants, and a granted tag must exist first. The built-in coder, researcher and scout workers use the store without extra setup.

## Limits

- The store lives in CLIO Coder's data directory on one host; `clio-coder store where` prints its folder. A worker on an SSH fleet node sees that node's own store.
- `put` copies bytes, and no backend keeps earlier versions of a blob.
- `clio-coder reset --data`, `reset --all` and `uninstall` without `--keep-data` delete the store for good.
- The store has been exercised on Linux only.
- The clio-core backend is experimental in 0.8.0 and needs a clio-core build from source. The full guide covers choosing it.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/exit-codes-and-output.html

# Automate with clio-coder run

Run one task from a script or CI job, read its exit code, and parse its JSON output.

## Run one task from a script

`clio-coder run` does one task without opening the terminal interface, then exits. The answer goes to stdout; progress, warnings and errors go to stderr, so a script can capture the answer alone.

```sh
clio-coder run --timeout 900 --max-cost-usd 2 "Run the test check and fix the failing parser test."
echo "exit $?"
```

Nobody is there to approve anything, so a request that would ask you is denied, and CLIO Coder continues another way or reports what it could not do. Name the actions the job needs in the prompt, such as "commit the fix", because the safety judge decides from your words.

## Read the exit code

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | The run finished. |
| `1` | The task failed, including a run that changed nothing because its actions were refused. |
| `2` | A usage error: an unknown flag, target or agent, or a refused admission or capability request. |
| `3` | A worker was stopped by permission refusals, or the safety judge kept blocking. |
| `4` | A spend ceiling stopped the run. |
| `124` | `--timeout` ran out. |
| `129`, `130`, `143` | A signal stopped the run (SIGHUP, SIGINT, SIGTERM). |

The full guide lists the codes other commands use.

## Bound the run

- `--timeout <seconds>` stops the run and exits 124.
- `--max-cost-usd <n>` caps what the run may spend on priced models.
- `--read-only` leaves every file outside CLIO Coder's own folders unchanged.
- `--autonomy yolo` lets an unattended job continue without waiting. It stays contained by default, and a call that would ask you is refused back to CLIO Coder, which continues without it.

## Read structured output

`--json` writes one JSON event per line on stdout: the session, the model's text, each tool call and the end of the turn. `--json-events terminal` keeps only the session header and the final result with its answer and exit code. Dispatch on each frame's `type` and ignore kinds you do not know, because new ones are added.

`clio-coder doctor --json`, `clio-coder targets --json`, `clio-coder models --json` and other commands print one JSON document for scripts as well.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/configuration-reference.html

# Configuration essentials

Find settings layers, save scopes, and the full configuration reference.

## Prefer the Settings Center

Use `/settings`, desktop **Settings**, or:

```sh
clio-coder configure --settings
```

Configure and desktop Settings share eight sections: Connections, Chat, Fleet, Context & Memory, Permissions & Limits, Appearance, Integrations, and Advanced. Terminal `/settings` groups the same controls into its own areas and lists the settings people change; every key still works in `settings.yaml`. The guided controls help you select a discovered model instead of typing a model ID. See [Connect a model](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html) for the walkthrough.

## Know where a change is saved

| Layer | File or scope |
| --- | --- |
| User defaults | `settings.yaml` in CLIO Coder's configuration directory |
| Shared project settings | `.clio-coder/settings.yaml` |
| Local project settings | `.clio-coder/settings.local.yaml` |
| Active session | The session/project/global choices offered by supported terminal controls |

Find the resolved locations on your machine:

```sh
clio-coder paths --json
```

`safety.sandbox` (`auto`, `required`, `off`) and `safety.sandboxNetwork` control the OS sandbox for dispatched native workers' commands and for your own session's shell commands at `default`. Objects merge by key; arrays and scalars replace the lower layer. Credential-bearing keys in project settings are ignored. Project saves require trusted project settings.

Saved routes seed a new session. A settings write from another process does not redirect a conversation already running; use that session's model controls.

## Look up an exact key

The full reference covers supported settings keys, defaults, CLI flags, project file ownership, and MCP trust. Use **Read the full guide** above or ask CLIO Coder to retrieve the relevant bundled documentation before editing YAML.

Settings validation is strict. For an older installation, `clio-coder upgrade` applies the registered migration and preserves a version-1 backup. For connection and installation diagnostics, use [doctor](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/doctor.html).

A session started in a repository subdirectory reads the repository's `.clio-coder/` settings, agents, skills, rules, hooks, and MCP servers. CLIO Coder writes an allow-list `.clio-coder/.gitignore`, so authored files can be committed while generated files stay out. A blanket `.clio-coder/` rule in your own `.gitignore` still hides them.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/environment-variables.html

# Environment essentials

Use directory overrides and existing provider credentials when needed.

## Use settings for ordinary preferences

Choose models, permissions, output style, and context behavior in [Settings](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html). Environment variables are useful when a script, container, or separate installation needs a different directory or an existing credential.

## Locate or separate installation state

```sh
clio-coder paths --json
```

| Variable | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `CLIO_CODER_HOME` | Set a shared root for CLIO Coder's directories |
| `CLIO_CODER_CONFIG_DIR` | Override the configuration directory |
| `CLIO_CODER_DATA_DIR` | Override the data directory |
| `CLIO_CODER_STATE_DIR` | Override the state directory |
| `CLIO_CODER_CACHE_DIR` | Override the cache directory |
| `CLIO_CODER_BIN_DIR` | Choose where the installer puts the `clio-coder` launcher (default `~/.local/bin`) |
| `CLIO_CODER_NODE_VERSION` | Choose the Node.js version the installer installs |

Individual directory overrides take precedence over the shared root. Separate state is useful for an isolated evaluation or a dedicated automation environment.

## How each directory is resolved

CLIO Coder resolves the config, data, state, and cache directories one at a time. The first match wins:

| Order | Source | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | The per-role variable | `CLIO_CODER_CONFIG_DIR` |
| 2 | The shared root | `CLIO_CODER_HOME` |
| 3 | Platform defaults | `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` on Linux, `APPDATA` or `LOCALAPPDATA` on Windows |

So you can keep everything under one root and still move only the cache elsewhere:

```sh
export CLIO_CODER_HOME="$HOME/clio-eval"
export CLIO_CODER_CACHE_DIR=/scratch/clio-cache
clio-coder paths --json
```

`clio-coder paths` creates nothing, so it is a safe way to confirm a layout before the first run. Scripts should parse its `--json` output rather than repeat these rules. With `CLIO_CODER_HOME` set, the installer root defaults to `$CLIO_CODER_HOME/install`; `CLIO_CODER_INSTALL_DIR` overrides it.

An isolated root still reads other coding agents' user skills and prompts from your real home. Set `CLIO_CODER_INTEROP_HOME=none` to read none of them, or a path to read another home.

## Credentials and terminal behavior

Supported providers can read their conventional credential variables, such as `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, or `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, when that provider is selected. Prefer CLIO Coder's managed authentication flow for normal interactive setup, and keep secrets out of project settings and transcripts.

| Variable | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| `OPENAI_API_KEY` | OpenAI |
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | Anthropic |
| `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | OpenRouter |
| `GEMINI_API_KEY` | Gemini |
| `AWS_*` | Bedrock credentials |
| `OLLAMA_API_KEY` | An Ollama target at `https://ollama.com` |

Google Vertex uses its application credentials. The managed alternative is `clio-coder auth`, with `auth login` and `auth status` per target.

`HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY`, and their lowercase forms apply to model requests, discovery probes, sign-in refreshes, and web fetches. `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` always go direct; name any other local model server in `NO_PROXY`. `clio-coder doctor` shows the proxy in effect.

`VISUAL` and `EDITOR` select an external editor, with `VISUAL` taking precedence. Terminal variables such as `TERM` and `COLORTERM` describe the environment; they do not grant tool permissions.

## Collect a trace

Debug toggles are off by default and turn on with `1`. `CLIO_CODER_TRACE_BOOT=1` turns on a boot-phase timing trace for a slow startup. The render trace takes a file path instead, and records timing but no conversation text:

```sh
CLIO_CODER_RENDER_TRACE="$PWD/render.jsonl" clio-coder
```

Setting it to `1` writes a file named `1` in the working directory.

The full guide lists provider-specific inputs, behavior overrides, and diagnostic switches. Use it when preparing automation or collecting a trace; most installations need no environment variables.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/system-one.html

# System One decision models

Bring a decision model, name a route, and read its limits.

## What it is

System One is an experimental way to bring a fast decision model to CLIO Coder. It is off by default and sends nothing until you name a route. The main agent then gets one tool, `consult`, and the route also drives a screen beside the safety judge and, when you turn it on, triage of queued messages. System One never answers you, never edits anything, and never removes a confirmation.

## Name a route

```sh
clio-coder systemone use jev
clio-coder systemone status
clio-coder systemone check jev --live
clio-coder systemone off
```

The choice takes effect on the next start. A list such as `jev,memory` is a failover order, and a route you did not name is never used. `run --systemone <route>` sets one headless run, and `/usage health` shows the status in a session.

| Route | What answers | What it needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `jev` | A hosted engine | `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` |
| `memory` | The model in `context.memory`, as labels | A memory target and model |
| `main` or a chat target | A chat route, as labels | That route's credentials |
| A declared engine | A decision server you run, with a named profile | An entry under `systemOne.engines` |

## The two consult forms

Only the main session gets `consult`, at most 3 calls per turn.

| Form | What the agent sends | What comes back |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Filter | Up to 256 files or items and one criterion | Ids and scores of matches |
| Questions | One to four `yesNo`, `pick`, or `rate` questions | Probabilities, or a label on an LLM route |

A filter sees a file as its path and a digest; use `grep` for behavior inside a body.

## The judge screen

When the safety judge reviews a call, System One asks whether the newest web and MCP results direct an AI agent. A positive reading can only turn a judge allow into a park on the approval card. LLM routes never screen.

## Declare an engine

```yaml
targets:
  - id: decider-gpu
    runtime: systemone
    url: http://127.0.0.1:13306/v1
    capabilities:
      contextWindow: 4096
systemOne:
  use: decider
  engines:
    decider:
      kind: systemone
      target: decider-gpu
      profile: strands-decider
```

You run the server. Name a profile: a `generic` engine never screens.

## When it fails

A failed ask returns nothing and the agent proceeds alone. Three timeouts in a row open a five-minute breaker; see `/usage health`.

## What to expect

`consult` filters a list against one criterion or asks typed questions, and the agent decides what to do with the answer. Between a third and more than half of filter matches can be wrong on the query sets tried so far, and nothing yet shows that `consult` helps. A hosted route receives what these uses send, including web and MCP result text at judge time. Redaction is best effort, so use a route you run yourself when that matters. An [information flow](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/information-flow.html) rule that excludes the engine's target ends that route as `flow-denied`, and nothing is sent.

Read [the research page](https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/system-one-decisions.html) for what has been measured and what is still open.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/information-flow.html

# Information flow

Keep named files away from destinations you did not choose.

## What it does

Information flow keeps named content, such as files under `secrets/`, away from destinations you did not choose. A source rule labels content when a session observes it, and the restrictions are checked before bytes leave for a model or a mediated outbound tool. It does nothing until a project declares rules and you approve them.

This controls where observed content may go. The safety model still decides whether a read or tool call may run.

## Declare and approve

Put `informationFlow` in the project's `.clio-coder/safety.yaml`, with each source naming its paths or tools and its allowed recipients. Then review and approve those exact bytes:

```sh
clio-coder config trust safety
clio-coder config trust safety --hash <reviewed-sha256>
clio-coder config trust safety --revoke
```

Restart CLIO Coder after approving. An unapproved edit can only forbid more.

Recipients can be a pinned model target, an exact endpoint, an origin, a pinned MCP server, or a named group. Follow [the tutorial](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/information-flow-rules.html) for a complete worked policy.

## Example policy

This policy keeps content under `secrets/` on one local model target:

```yaml
version: 1
informationFlow:
  targets:
    local:
      runtime: llamacpp
      endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1
  recipients:
    private-models: ["target:local"]
  sources:
    - id: secrets-local
      paths: [secrets/]
      recipients: ["group:private-models"]
```

After approval and restart, reading `secrets/notes.txt` labels the session. Requests to the `local` target still go out; switching to a cloud target refuses the next request before it sends. `recipients: []` forbids every transfer.

The first `config trust safety` command is read-only and prints the digest to approve. After `--revoke`, rules left in the file label content without allowing any recipient.

## What acquires a label

Read tools such as `read`, `grep`, and `find` label matching paths, including sources below a directory they walk. Bash commands and `@file` references label the paths they name; reads hidden in scripts or variables are not reliably seen.

Labels belong to the session and survive compaction, resume, handoffs, and worker results. Changing the policy, the model, or the autonomy mode does not clear them. Files the session writes carry no label.

## Read a refusal and recover

A refusal names the rule, the source path or tool, the requested destination, and any allowed recipients.

| Refusal | Recovery |
| --- | --- |
| Destination is outside the rule's recipients | Switch to an allowed destination, or start a new session |
| Rule was unapproved when content was read | Approve the exact bytes and restart |
| Approved rule names no recipient | Start a new session for work that must leave |
| Runtime cannot admit its own model requests | Use a native HTTP target, or add its pinned target to every rule |

Claude Code, Codex, and other external runtimes are refused whenever a rule does not allow their pinned target. At `yolo`, mediated outbound tools skip the label check, but model requests are still checked.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/glossary.html

# Glossary

Plain-language meanings of the words CLIO Coder uses, from target to worktree.

## Words you meet first

Each term below in a sentence or two, with the guide that explains it. The full guide then gives the precise definitions, mapped to the source types that own them.

## Sessions and models

| Term | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| Session | One conversation with CLIO Coder in a project. It is saved, so you can resume it later. See [Commands and modes](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/commands-and-modes.html). |
| Target (connection) | A place CLIO Coder sends prompts to: a provider account or a local model server, with its default model. Settings call it a connection. See [Configuration and targets](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html). |
| Chat route | The target and model your main conversation uses right now. |
| Compaction | Shortening a long conversation into a summary so it fits the model's context window. See [Context continuity](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/context-continuity.html). |
| Handbook | `CLIO-CODER.md` at the repository root: the project's name, conventions and rules, written by you and kept in Git. |
| Memory | Notes CLIO Coder keeps while you work, such as your requirements and what failed, so it can remind the agent later. See [Proactive memory](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/proactive-memory.html). |
| Doctor | `clio-coder doctor`, a read-only check of your install, connections and sandbox. See [Doctor](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/doctor.html). |

## Safety

| Term | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| Autonomy level | How much CLIO Coder may do without you: `default` asks when something is risky, `yolo` never waits for you. See [Sandbox and safety](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/sandbox-and-safety.html). |
| Sandbox | An operating-system wall around shell commands. Inside it a command can write only to the project and scratch folders and cannot read your credentials. |
| Contained | A command that runs inside the sandbox. At `default` most contained work runs without asking. |
| Safety judge | A model that checks a risky call against what you asked for, before you are asked. It allows it, refuses it, or passes it to you. |
| Approval card | The question CLIO Coder shows when a call needs your answer. One nobody answers is denied after a timeout. |
| Snapshot | A private copy of your files that CLIO Coder takes before it changes them. `/rewind` restores one. |

## Workers and results

| Term | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| Worker | A separate agent that does one task for the main session, often on its own branch. See [Fleet dispatch](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/fleet-dispatch.html). |
| Fleet | The workers available to you and the routes they run on. |
| Dispatch | Handing a task to a worker, with `/run` in a session or `clio-coder run --agent` from a shell. |
| Worktree | A separate checkout of your repository on its own branch, where a worker can change files without touching yours. |
| Run record | The sealed record of a finished worker run: what it did, what it changed and which checks passed. `/view verify <runId>` checks it. |
| Check (verifier) | A command in `.clio-coder/verifiers.yaml` that decides whether work is right, such as a test suite or a benchmark. |
| Peer | Another coding agent, such as Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode, that CLIO Coder hands a task to. See [Coding agent interoperability](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/interop.html). |
| Store | A place outside your working tree for result files and datasets, shared by every checkout of the project. See [Store](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/store.html). |
| Research campaign | A loop where the agent tries one change at a time and keeps it only when a measured number improves and every check still passes. See [Research and arena](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/research-and-arena.html). |
| Arena match | The same task given to several models, each result run through the same check, so you can compare them and vote blind. |
| Sweep | A set of run directories for one experiment, each checked on its own. See [Slurm](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/slurm.html). |

## Packages

| Term | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| Skill | Written instructions for a procedure, in a `SKILL.md` file, that the agent loads when the task needs it. |
| Prompt template | A saved prompt you run as a slash command, such as `/bugfix`. |
| Library | The installable packages CLIO Coder knows about, browsed with `/library`. See [Library packages](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/resource-library.html). |
| Plugin | A package of content only: skills, prompts, agents and playbooks. Installing one never runs code. See [Plugins](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/plugins.html). |
| Extension | A package of code that changes CLIO Coder itself. It runs in its own process, after you review what it may do. See [Extensions](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/harness-extensions.html). |

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/semantic-context.html

# Semantic context

Search your project by meaning with a local embedding route.

## What it does

Semantic context is a beta local search index for code maps, wiki pages, approved memory, authorized evidence, recorded worker output, and folders you register. It uses a separate embedding target. It starts disabled, and ordinary startup scans and embeds nothing until you configure it.

## Set it up and search

Create a target for an embedding route you already run. CLIO Coder does not start a server for it. Then configure, refresh, and search:

```sh
clio-coder semantic configure --help
clio-coder semantic inbox preview ./experiment-data
clio-coder semantic inbox add ./experiment-data --id experiments
clio-coder semantic refresh
clio-coder semantic status
clio-coder semantic search "Which run produced the delayed oscillation?" --limit 5
```

`--qualify` checks that a route accepts requests and returns vectors of the right shape. It does not check retrieval quality. A result is a candidate to read, and it does not prove anything by itself.

Follow [the tutorial](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/semantic-context-and-recordings.html) for a full walkthrough.

## Configure the embedding model

`configure` pins a target, model, and asset identity. Prefer a `sha256:<hash>` of the model file; a plain label is reported as unverified.

```sh
clio-coder semantic configure \
  --target litellm --model mini/embeddinggemma-2-q8 \
  --asset-identity sha256:<gguf-sha256> \
  --modality text --modality image \
  --qualify
```

`--background`, off by default, allows refreshes at session start and after code map changes. Run `clio-coder semantic qualify` again after changing the serving build or model.

## Register inboxes

`inbox add` previews the work before saving a folder, which stays private to its project unless you pass `--scope user`. Ignore files and the project's read policy apply, and symlinks and credential-shaped files are refused. `inbox list` and `inbox remove <id>` manage them. An interrupted `refresh` keeps the last complete generation.

## Search and ask

| Filter | Narrows to |
| --- | --- |
| `--kind` | `code`, `wiki`, `memory`, `evidence`, `inbox`, or `recording`; repeatable |
| `--run <id>` | One parent run |
| `--since`, `--until` | Source dates, inclusive |
| `--media-type <MIME>` | One media type |

Search returns five results by default and at most 20, each with a path and a line, page, or timestamp. In a session, ask a specific question; the agent searches the same index, then reads the source. Worker output saved with `clio-coder run --agent <id> --record` is searchable as `recording`.

## Change the model

A new profile gets its own index. `clio-coder semantic reembed --profile <id>` rebuilds it; add `--from <old-profile-sha256>` to embed the previous profile's records. Old vectors are never copied.

## When something fails

If the embedding route is down, search returns lexical candidates from the last complete generation. Video frames need a qualified image route and `ffmpeg` on PATH. Scanned PDFs, raw video, and audio other than mono 16 kHz WAV are not indexed.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/built-in-agents.html

# Built-in and custom agents

See the agents you can dispatch and add your own.

## See the agents

CLIO Coder dispatches focused agents from Markdown recipes. Each recipe declares the agent's tools, budget, and the result it must return.

```sh
clio-coder agents
clio-coder agents validate
clio-coder run --agent coder "<task>"
```

`clio-coder agents` lists the agents you can run, including `architect`, `coder`, `debugger`, `documenter`, `git-master`, `tester`, and `verifier`. `/run` dispatches one from a session. Add `--read-only` to deny writes, commands, and delegation for one dispatch.

Helper agents such as Scout are dispatched by the main agent, and `clio-coder agents --all` lists them. You cannot start them directly.

## Shipped agents

| Agent | Use it to | Edits files |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `architect` | Design a change or cut a plan into a sprint | Plan file only |
| `coder` | Make a bounded change, repair, or refactor | Yes |
| `debugger` | Diagnose failing code, tests, or runs | No |
| `documenter` | Write docs and examples from source | Yes |
| `git-master` | Commits, worktrees, merges, pull requests | Yes |
| `tester` | Add deterministic regression tests | Yes |
| `verifier` | Run test, lint, build, and review gates | No |
| `wiki-writer` | Plan a wiki or write one page | Yes |
| `wiki-repair` | Fix one wiki draft's diagnostics | Yes |

## Add your own

Put a recipe at `.clio-coder/agents/<id>.md` for one project, or in the `agents` folder of your CLIO Coder config directory for yourself. The file name is the agent's id, and when a user recipe and a project recipe share an id, the project one wins. Run `clio-coder agents validate` after an edit.

A recipe must declare every required key, and `audience` must be `custom`:

```md
---
version: 1
name: My Agent
description: Focused local review helper.
tools:
  required: [read, artifact]
  optional: [grep, find, ls, git]
skills: []
audience: custom
category: quality
capabilityClass: artifact-write
latencyClass: balanced
projectContextTier: bounded
budget: {toolCalls: 20, readReserve: 4, synthesis: true}
resultContract: {kind: artifact-report}
tags: [review]
---

You are My Agent. Inspect only the requested area. Never edit files.
```

The body is the agent's instructions. Model and target are chosen at dispatch, not in the recipe. Start it with `clio-coder run --agent my-agent "Review the parser change."`. A user recipe may replace a shipped agent such as `coder`; a project recipe cannot.

## What validation rejects

`clio-coder agents validate` checks project and user recipes and skills, and the fleet bindings in `.clio-coder/settings.local.yaml`. It prints each problem as a `file: field: message` line and exits 1 when there is any. It rejects an unknown or missing key, an audience other than `custom`, a `budget` whose `readReserve` is not below `toolCalls`, a skill that does not resolve, and tools that break the `capabilityClass`, such as a `verification` agent that uses `bash`. A rejected recipe is not loaded.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/first-session.html

# Your first session with CLIO Coder

> Connect a model, open a repository, and ask CLIO Coder to explain how it builds and runs its tests.

CLIO Coder works in the repository you open. For your first session, give it a small, concrete task: explain how the project builds and runs its tests. That lets you see how it reads code and uses tools before asking it to make a change.

**Version scope**

This tutorial describes v0.8.0. The recordings on this page come from a small JavaScript project with one failing test and Qwen 3.8 27B on a local model server. The first starts with no model configured. The install step was not recorded.

## 1. Install CLIO Coder

The installer brings its own Node.js and needs no root. Linux, macOS, and WSL are the primary platforms. Native Windows is best effort, so use the current stable release. On Linux, the installer offers to add the desktop app when it finishes.

```sh
curl -fsSL https://coder.iowarp.ai/install.sh | sh
```

## 2. Connect a model

Open a terminal in a repository you know and start CLIO Coder:

```sh
cd /path/to/your/project
clio-coder
```

With no model configured, setup starts on its own:

```text
No model target is configured. Clio needs a model before it can do anything else, so setup starts now.
```

Setup looks for a provider key in your environment, a stored sign-in and a local model server, and lists what it found. Pick one, or choose **Set up something else** and answer what you have: an API key, a subscription, a model server or gateway, or a setup file from your lab or team. Use a model that supports tool calling.

CLIO Coder sends the model one short test request and saves only when it answers; a browser sign-in you complete is the exception. In the recording, setup found a model server and saved it:

```text
◇  Testing litellm / qwen3.8-27b ... answered in 0.4 s.
◇  target litellm saved, runtime litellm
◇  chat runs on litellm, model qwen3.8-27b
◇  fleet default is litellm
◇  settings written to ~/.config/clio-coder/settings.yaml
◇  Saved. Chat and workers use this model. Change it any time with /model or /config.
```

`clio-coder configure` runs setup again at any time. Its **Connect by endpoint** is the shortcut when you already know the URL. LM Studio commonly serves at `http://localhost:1234`; Ollama commonly serves at `http://localhost:11434`. The [connection guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html) covers setup and credentials.

If you have used CLIO Coder before, you can skip this step. A chat route you already chose stays in use, and CLIO Coder will not swap it for another when it stops working.

If a connection fails, run:

```sh
clio-coder doctor
```

## 3. Open a workspace

When setup saves, the terminal workspace opens in the same folder. In the recording, its header read `Model      litellm · qwen3.8-27b` and the status line ended `200K ctx`, the context window of the model it found. Later, `clio-coder` opens the workspace directly.

Or open the desktop alpha in your browser:

```sh
clio-coder gui --open
```

In the desktop, open a workspace folder and start a task. If you have not configured a model, **Guided setup** is also available in the browser; terminal configuration is optional. For this tutorial, either interface gives you a place to enter the first request.

## 4. Ask a focused question

Try this request:

> Explain how this repository builds and runs its tests. Identify the main entry points and suggest one verification task. Do not change files yet.

Follow the tool activity as CLIO Coder reads the repository. The recording ends while it plans its first reads. If an approval card appears, read the call before allowing it. If the answer misses an important directory or build system, name it in a follow-up.

## 5. Make the next task specific

Once you understand the project, ask for one change you can check. Name the problem, what to do and how to verify it. The recording below gave this request for the project's one failing test:

> The absolute-zero test fails. Find the cause, fix it, and run the test check.

![Terminal recording of a first task in CLIO Coder 0.8.0: asked why the absolute-zero test fails, the agent reads the source, changes kelvin <= 0 to kelvin < 0 in temperature.mjs, runs the declared test check with exit 0, and reports that all seven tests pass and that negative Kelvin is still rejected.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/cast-first-task.webp)

*A first task at default autonomy: the agent finds an off-by-one guard, edits it, and runs the project's declared test check without asking.*

[Recording (asciicast)](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/casts/cast-first-task.cast), 0:27. Transcript:

```text
A first task in CLIO Coder: fix a failing test and verify
Recorded with CLIO Coder 0.8.0. Each section is the terminal screen at that moment.

== ready

~/projects/calibration-lab $ clio-coder
Clio Coder: terminal panes are not installed. Install them with `clio-coder panes install`.
┌─ >C_ Clio Coder v0.8.0 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Model      litellm · qwen3.8-27b                                                                                     │
│ Autonomy   Default · reviewed approvals                                                                              │
│ Awareness  Not indexed yet                                                                                           │
│ ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌ │
│ /context init to index this repo                                                                                     │
```

Use your project's real test name. Read the diff and the check output yourself before you commit the change.

## Keep going

In the terminal, `/help` lists commands, `/model` selects a model, `/settings` opens the settings center, and `/config` opens your connections, where **Add a target** runs setup again without leaving the session.

When you quit, CLIO Coder prints a summary of the session and a `/resume <id>` line. Start `clio-coder` again and type that line to return to the conversation, or use `/resume` alone to pick from a list.

The [commands guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/commands-and-modes.html) covers shortcuts and session controls. The [tools guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/tool-usage.html) explains the repository tools and their permissions.

- [Let CLIO Coder work without watching every call](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/let-it-work-with-containment-and-rewind.html)
- [A numerical change, checked with CLIO Coder](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/temperature-calibration.html)

# Desktop or terminal: find your workspace

> See both interfaces, learn how to launch them, and choose where to start your next coding session.

CLIO Coder has two interfaces to the same runtime. The terminal offers the primary workflow. The desktop alpha opens locally in your browser and gives you a visual workspace for projects and conversations.

## CLIO Coder in the terminal

Open your repository and launch CLIO Coder:

```sh
cd /path/to/your/project
clio-coder
```

![CLIO Coder terminal at start: the CLIO Coder wordmark beside the selected model and autonomy, the workspace with its Git state, and the composer reporting the Qwen 3.8 model ready.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/tui-boot.webp)

The terminal combines the conversation, tool calls, permissions, and worker activity. Type `/help` to see available commands, or `/model` to choose a model.

![CLIO Coder in the terminal changing one line of temperature.mjs to fix a failing test, then running the declared test check through verify with exit 0](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/tui-verify.webp)

Each tool call stays on its own line with its result, so you can see what ran before you read the answer. `/view` opens the recorded calls and their output.

During a turn, **Enter** queues a message that CLIO Coder reads at the next pause between tool calls, **Alt+S** sends it now, and **Escape** cancels the run.

On a permission card, **Enter** allows the call. **Esc** denies it, which skips that call and leaves the run going. **Alt+X** stops the turn.

## CLIO Coder on the desktop

From a terminal, run:

```sh
clio-coder gui --open
```

The command opens the local application with its access link. Open a workspace folder, describe a task, and choose a model and thinking level from the composer.

The rail on the left groups tasks by workspace. The Session column on the right shows the workspace's Git state, the model, context, usage, the plan, artifacts, changes, and run records as the task runs.

You can keep any number of tasks open in one window. Launching again brings that window forward under WSL, when the app is installed through Chrome or Edge, and on a Linux desktop with `wmctrl`, `xdotool` or sway when the background app is running. Otherwise it opens a new browser tab.

Up to four turns run at once by default, set by `interface.guiTurnCapacity` from 1 to 16, and later ones wait for a slot. A task with no turn running and no window showing it for five minutes is paused with its conversation kept, and opening it again brings it back. A task you never typed into closes instead.

With the default **Ask first** setting, CLIO Coder reads, edits files in the workspace, and runs commands it recognizes, such as read-only inspection and the project's test runners, without stopping. An unrecognized shell command, a large dispatch plan, or anything that publishes outside the project waits for you. The approval names the call, what allowing it authorizes, and what it can affect.

The same control can be switched to **Run without asking** for one task after a second confirmation. The cards stop, and by default the sandbox, snapshots, and safety judge stay on. A turn that changed files ends with a card that opens the changes for review. Type `/` in the composer to list session commands.

A first run with no model connection opens on guided setup, which asks the same questions as `clio-coder configure`.

![CLIO Coder desktop new-task view with the calibration-lab workspace, recent tasks, a message composer, three starter prompts, and the Overview column.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/gui-home.webp)

*Start another task in the open workspace, with recent tasks kept in the left rail.*

![CLIO Coder desktop after a completed calibration task: seven passing tests and the reference temperatures in the conversation, with task status, workspace, model, context and usage in the Session column.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/gui-task.webp)

*A completed desktop task: test results, reference temperatures, and the Session column alongside the conversation.*

![CLIO Coder desktop waiting for approval to run npm run check: the command, authorization, consequences, Reject and Allow once controls, with task activity and context in the Session column.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/gui-approval.webp)

*Review a project check before allowing its command to run.*

![CLIO Coder desktop setup welcome, with Provider, Connect, Model, Test and Workspace steps, the CLIO Coder mark, and Get started.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/gui-setup.webp)

*A fresh desktop profile opens guided setup before a connection is saved.*

The desktop from a new task to a finished one: the composer, the answer with its tool calls, a waiting approval, and guided setup.

The desktop is in alpha and covers a subset of terminal workflows. Treat it as an optional way to use CLIO Coder, and keep the terminal available for commands that the desktop does not yet expose.

On Linux with a systemd user session, you can install the optional background application, which starts at login and appears in your app menu. The installer offers the same step, and `--gui` accepts it without asking:

```sh
clio-coder gui background install --open
```

For an optional Linux desktop entry, run `clio-coder gui launcher install`. The background service and launcher each have an `uninstall` command. The [desktop app guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/gui.html) covers those options.

## Choose where to begin

Start in the terminal if you work mostly from a shell or need the primary set of CLIO Coder workflows. Start on the desktop if you prefer browsing projects and working with attachments in a visual interface.

Both launch commands use the installed CLIO Coder package. You do not need an account on this website. Your model connections use your own local server, institutional endpoint, or cloud provider.

Try [a temperature-calibration example with recorded checks](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/temperature-calibration.html), or follow [your first session](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/first-session.html) for a concrete task to try in either workspace.

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/let-it-work-with-containment-and-rewind.html

# Let CLIO Coder work without watching every call

> Check the sandbox, undo a change with /rewind, tell the safety judge about your machine, and know when yolo is the right call.

Most of a coding task should not need you. At the `default` level, CLIO Coder runs shell work inside an OS sandbox, snapshots your files before it changes them, and has a safety judge review what escapes the sandbox. You are asked only when the judge has no verdict or the decision is yours.

This guide shows how to check that setup, undo a change, and choose when to step up to `yolo`.

**Version scope**

This guide describes v0.8.0. The sandbox needs bubblewrap on Linux; on macOS it uses an experimental `sandbox-exec` profile. Snapshots need a Git work tree. Native Windows has neither guarantee, so read what `doctor` reports on your host.

## Before you start

- CLIO Coder installed, with a connected model.
- A Git repository you can experiment in, with a clean working tree.

### Check what this host can contain

```sh
clio-coder doctor
```

Look for the `shell sandbox` row. It names the backend and where contained commands may write. If no backend exists, commands outside the recognized set go to the judge and then to you, so the rest of this guide still holds with more questions.

A contained command can write the workspace, the scratch roots, `/tmp`, and a private tool cache. Your own `~/.cache` and `~/.npm` stay read-only. Credentials, credential variables, secret files such as `.env`, and the SSH agent are hidden, new local Unix sockets are refused, and the network stays on. A directory your scripts must always write belongs in `safety.scratchRoots`.

A secret path is also refused before any sandbox is involved. In the recording below, asked `Show me the API token in .env.`, the agent tried `ls -la .env 2>&1 | head`, and CLIO Coder stopped it:

```text
rule: secret_path_bash
This is a hard block; confirmation cannot override it.
```

![Terminal recording in which the user asks CLIO Coder for the API token in the project's .env. The agent's ls -la .env command is blocked under rule secret_path_bash as a hard block that confirmation cannot override, and the agent answers that it cannot show the token and gives the command to view it in the user's own terminal.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/cast-sandbox.webp)

*The project's .env is refused outright; confirmation cannot override the block.*

```text
Alt+M Model · ? Keys
```

### Give it a task and watch what happens

On a scratch branch, type this:

```text
Delete the build output directory, regenerate it, and run the project's test check. Report what you ran.
```

Workspace edits and contained commands run without a card. A delete inside the workspace runs after a snapshot is taken. Build output is usually gitignored, and a snapshot does not hold ignored files, so the build directory itself is not something `/rewind` can bring back. A push or a command that leaves the sandbox goes to the judge first.

### Undo it with /rewind

```text
/rewind
```

The list shows this session's snapshots, newest first, with how many files each differs by. `Enter` previews a restore before anything is written. Confirming takes one more snapshot, so the rewind itself can be rewound. `Esc` goes back without writing anything.

In the recorded session behind this guide, the regenerated build was gitignored and nothing tracked had changed, so the preview read:

```text
The workspace already matches this snapshot. Nothing would change.
```

It also said that gitignored files are never touched and that the Git index, `HEAD` and branches do not change.

### Tell the judge about your machine

The judge reads your typed messages and the proposed call. It never reads the agent's reasoning or tool output, so text in a file cannot argue past it. Name what is yours in your user settings, the `settings.yaml` file in the folder that `clio-coder paths` prints on its `config` line:

```yaml title=settings.yaml
safety:
  judge:
    environment:
      - "Shared cluster; /scratch/$USER is mine to create and delete in."
    allow:
      - "restarting the dev containers this project's compose file defines"
```

**What you should see**

Contained work runs without a card, and `/rewind` lists a snapshot from before the first change of the turn. This shows the controls work on your host. It does not show that the agent's change is correct, so review the diff and the check results.

## What still reaches you

Some decisions never go to the judge: `ask_user` questions, CLIO Coder's own settings, a plan-scale dispatch, and a model edit of project settings. An approval card nobody answers within `safety.unattendedAfterSeconds` (300 by default) is denied, never approved, and the turn continues. A question nobody answers takes its recommended option, and `/decisions` shows what was chosen for you.

## When to use yolo

`yolo` is for long jobs you leave running: nothing waits for you. It is contained by default. The sandbox, snapshots, and safety judge work as at `default`, and a call that would have asked you is refused back to CLIO Coder, so the job keeps going without it.

```sh
clio-coder --autonomy yolo
```

The first interactive activation shows a one-time acceptance card, and yolo is refused as root outside a detected container. A short floor still blocks deleting your home directory or a system tree, `mkfs`, writes to a block device, fork bombs, and reads of CLIO Coder's credential store. Your project's approved rules and the run's ceilings also hold. Snapshots stay on.

After 600 tool calls since you last spoke, set by `safety.limits.autonomousToolCalls`, the session pauses until you continue.

Unconfined yolo is the skip-permissions mode for a container or another disposable environment: nothing asks, and commands run unsandboxed with your credentials. It takes effect only with `safety.yoloConfinement: unconfined` in your user settings and its own one-time acceptance. The footer shows which one is active.

To keep unconfined yolo inside the sandbox, also set `safety.sandbox: required`. Commands then run contained, and a retry with `unsandboxed: true` is refused. An outward command such as `git push` or `gh pr create` leaves the sandbox only as one literal command on that tool's short option list, with no pipe, redirect, or substitution. `doctor` reports which rule applies.

| | `default` | `yolo`, contained | `yolo`, unconfined |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Shell commands | In the OS sandbox when a backend exists | As at `default` | Unsandboxed as you, unless `safety.sandbox: required` |
| Would-be approvals | Judge first, then you | Judge first, then refused back to CLIO Coder | None |
| Your questions | Wait, then resolve after the timeout | Answered at once | Answered at once |
| Workers | Own sandbox, asks go to the judge | Dispatched as at `default` | Own sandbox, run the yolo way in their scope |
| `/rewind` | Available | Available | Available |

**What this does not protect**

- The sandbox contains `bash`, `run_script` and checks that run commands through `verify`. Typed `write` and `edit` calls follow the rules instead.
- Ignored files, untracked files over 16 MiB, and nested repositories are not in a snapshot.
- `/rewind` restores files. It never moves refs: it prints the commands that bring a moved branch back.
- The judge is a model. It can be wrong, and a route error means no verdict, so the call parks or is denied.
- Stronger isolation needs an external sandbox such as a container.

**Next steps**

- [Check a change against your repository](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/check-a-change-against-your-repository.html)
- [Tools and permissions](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/tool-usage.html)
- [Keep a long coding task on track](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/keep-long-coding-tasks-on-track.html)

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/run-a-playbook-and-land-it.html

# Run a playbook from plan to commit

> Run the builtin sdlc playbook on one task, watch it work, and read the three commits it makes on your branch.

A playbook is a sequence of workers and code steps that the fleet runs for you. The builtin `sdlc` playbook plans, builds, tests with a bounded fix loop, reviews with a bounded revise loop, and documents, with three commits along the way. This guide runs it on one task and reads what it committed on your branch.

**Version scope**

This guide describes v0.8.0. Run time and cost depend on your repository and the model you connect, so start with a small task.

## Before you start

- CLIO Coder installed, with a connected model that supports tool calling.
- A clean Git repository with a test command.
- A small, specific task you could review by hand.

### See what is available

```sh
clio-coder playbook list
```

`sdlc` shows as `setup` until the project declares the two commands it runs, `test` and `commit`.

### Declare the commands it runs

```sh
clio-coder playbook commands init
```

This drafts `.clio-coder/playbooks/commands.yaml` from your project's declarations, fully commented out, because uncommenting an entry confirms its exact command. Edit it to name what this project runs:

```yaml title=.clio-coder/playbooks/commands.yaml
version: 1
commands:
  test:
    argv: ["npm", "run", "test"]
  commit:
    argv: ["git", "commit", "-m", "{{commitMessage}}"]
```

### Check before you run

```sh
clio-coder playbook validate sdlc --var task="Add empty-input handling to the parser"
clio-coder playbook graph sdlc --var task="Add empty-input handling to the parser"
```

`validate` runs the execution preflight and `graph` prints the compiled waves, loops, scopes, and write boundaries, both without side effects. It resolves agents, targets, and profiles, and checks the session budget and write boundaries. A failed preflight during a real run exits 2 before anything dispatches.

### Run it

```sh
clio-coder fleet run sdlc --var task="Add empty-input handling to the parser"
```

The first line, on stderr, names the fleet root and plan hash. Each settled step prints one line. In another terminal, `clio-coder fleet status` shows the board and `clio-coder fleet events <root> --follow` follows the journal.

The steps work in your checkout, one after another, not in separate worktrees. The `suite` loop runs your `test` command inside the sandbox, rooted at the checkout, up to three times, and hands each of the first two failures back to the coder.

The command exits 0 only when every required step succeeded, no step was skipped, and every loop resolved. Any other finished run exits 1. A failed preflight, or an error in the scheduler itself, exits 2.

### Read what it committed

```sh
git log --oneline -3
git show --stat HEAD~2 HEAD~1 HEAD
```

The three `commit` steps commit the plan, the code, and the docs on the branch you have checked out, so there is nothing to merge or land afterwards. If you do not want the result, reset the branch to where it was before the run.

`clio-coder fleet land` is for something else: the task branch a worker dispatched with its own worktree keeps when its change was not merged.

![Terminal output: playbook validate sdlc reports 8 declared steps, 6 code steps, 4 agents and 14 plan steps with the plan hash; playbook graph lists waves 1 to 14 with each step's kind, agent or command, and scope, then the suite and review loops.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/cli-playbook-graph.webp)

*validate runs the preflight and graph prints the compiled waves and loops, both without side effects.*

**What you should see**

A summary with each loop's terminal reason and any steps that need your decision, and three new commits on your branch. A finished run shows the playbook ran and its checks passed. It does not show the change is right, so read the diff.

## Make it yours

```sh
clio-coder playbook new parser-fix --from sdlc
```

This copies the builtin to `.clio-coder/playbooks/parser-fix.md`, where you can change steps, agents, and limits. A resumed run replays a completed prefix of the same plan: `clio-coder fleet run <name> --resume <runId>`.

**Boundaries**

- Under `fleet run` nobody is attached, so a worker's ordinary ask is denied, not judged.
- One lock per Git checkout keeps two fleets out of the same workspace.
- `clio-coder telemetry verify --run <run-id>` checks the record of a run. The journals are hash-chained and unsigned, so they show consistency, not who wrote them.

**Next steps**

- [Workers and fleets](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/fleet-dispatch.html)
- [See what a session cost and what a run did](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/see-what-a-session-cost-and-what-a-run-did.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/run-it-unattended-within-limits.html

# Run it unattended within limits

> Start a headless run with a cost ceiling and a timeout, ask read-only questions, schedule turns, and know what stops each one.

You can start a task and leave. Headless `clio-coder run` does one turn with nobody attached, and the limits you set are enforced. This guide covers a bounded headless run, a read-only one, the timeouts that apply when you walk away from an open session, and scheduled turns.

**Version scope**

This guide describes v0.8.0. A headless run has no one to ask: it denies whatever the safety judge does not allow, and `ask_user` is not available.

## Before you start

- CLIO Coder installed, with a connected model.
- A Git repository, and a task you can state completely in one prompt.

### Put your decisions in the prompt

The judge reads only your prompt in a headless run, so name the actions the job needs:

```sh
clio-coder run --max-cost-usd 2 --timeout 1800 \
  "Fix the failing parser test, run the test check, and commit on this branch. Do not push."
```

`--max-cost-usd` caps the priced spend this run adds. Reaching it stops the run and its workers with exit 4 and `budget_ceiling`. Calls already in flight can pass the cap, and unpriced routes cannot be bounded, so pair it with `--timeout`, which exits 124 on expiry. The session ceiling, 5 USD by default, still applies.

### Ask a question that cannot change anything

```sh
clio-coder run --read-only "Which modules have no tests? Report paths."
```

`--read-only` is an enforced ceiling on the main agent, not a request. No file outside CLIO Coder's home changes: writes are refused, and shell commands run only in a read-only sandbox.

### Stream it to another program

```sh
clio-coder run --json "Summarize the last five commits."
```

The stream opens with a `session` header carrying its schema version and ends with one `run_end` frame carrying the exit code and outcome. Read the result from that frame. Continue later with `--continue` or `--session <id prefix>`.

### Walk away from an open session

In the terminal, an unanswered approval card is denied after `safety.unattendedAfterSeconds` (300 by default) and the turn continues. A question takes its recommended option. Any key stops the countdown. When you return, `/decisions` shows what was chosen, and the exit summary counts it on an `Unattended` line.

### Schedule turns while idle

```text
/loop 30m Check the nightly build log and report anything new.
/loop 5m --command make check
/loop
```

A bare `/loop` lists the jobs. A loop runs only while its conversation is idle and never replays missed runs. The `--command` form polls a program directly, with no shell.

**What you should see**

A finished turn with its exit code, not a parked prompt. An exit of 4 means the cost ceiling stopped it. `clio-coder telemetry why-stopped <session>` explains a stop afterward.

## Read how a run ended

Stderr names the session and ends with an `observed:` line that counts tool calls, refusals, writes, and checks. When `--max-cost-usd` meets a route with no price, stderr says the cap cannot bound it; declare `targets[].pricing` to fix that. A script should read the exit code or the `run_end` frame, not the prose answer.

In a separate run of the first step, made for this guide apart from the session at the top of the page, Qwen 3.8 27B worked on a repository with one failing parser test. It fixed the parser, ran the test, committed on the branch, and pushed nothing. Stderr read:

```text
clio-coder run: --max-cost-usd does not bound unpriced routes: litellm/qwen3.8-27b; declare targets[].pricing to bound them
clio-coder run: session sjajclvyg6cw
clio-coder run: observed: 10 tool calls, 0 refused · 1 write · checks passed: npm run test, git diff
```

A `--json` run of the third step from the same set ended with this frame:

```json
{"type":"run_end","startedAt":"2026-11-12T19:02:57.365Z","endedAt":"2026-11-12T19:03:09.119Z","exitCode":0,"outcome":"succeeded","safety":{"decisions":{"allowed":3,"blocked":0,"permissionRequested":0},"blockedAttempts":[]}}
```

| Exit | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | The run settled and succeeded |
| `1` | It failed: the model was unreachable, a worker did not deliver, or a refused call left the task undone |
| `2` | A usage error, including `--autonomy yolo` as root outside a container |
| `3` | At `yolo`, the safety judge blocked too many calls in a row; review the run, then `--continue` |
| `4` | A cost ceiling, or at `yolo` an autonomous cap on tool calls, minutes, or tokens, stopped it; `--continue` resumes |
| `124` | `--timeout` expired; the run still settled and sealed |
| `130`, `143` | Ctrl+C or a SIGTERM stopped it |

## Pick the right tool

| When you want | Use | What still stops it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One bounded task | `clio-coder run` at `default` | Judge, sandbox, cost ceiling, timeout |
| A long job you leave running | `clio-coder run --autonomy yolo` | Contained by default: the sandbox and judge stay on, and a call the judge does not allow is refused back to the run. Ceilings, timeout, the loop guard, and the tool budget also stop it |
| A recurring check | `/loop` in an open session | Pause or stop it; needs the session to stay open |

**Boundaries**

- A contained command starts without credential variables and cannot open secret files, so name tools that need them. CLIO Coder may rerun with `unsandboxed: true`, which the judge reviews. At unconfined `yolo` under `safety.sandbox: required`, that retry is refused.
- `yolo` does not carry over from `settings.yaml` to a headless run. It comes only from that run's own `--autonomy yolo`, and it exits 2 as root outside a detected container.

**Next steps**

- [Let CLIO Coder work without watching every call](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/let-it-work-with-containment-and-rewind.html)
- [Report a problem without leaking your machine](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/report-a-problem-without-leaking-your-machine.html)
- [Commands and shortcuts](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/commands-and-modes.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/see-what-a-session-cost-and-what-a-run-did.html

# See what a session cost and what a run did

> Read session cost and stop reasons from local journals, verify a sealed record, and prepare an archive that uploads nothing.

CLIO Coder records what each process, session, and worker run did in local journals, and every usage figure on every surface comes from those journals. This guide shows how to read a session's cost, find out why it stopped, check a run's record, and prepare an archive for a maintainer.

**Version scope**

This guide describes v0.8.0. Costs are shown with their provenance: a measured figure, an estimate, and an unknown value stay separate. An unknown stays unknown rather than becoming zero.

## Before you start

- CLIO Coder installed, and at least one finished session in a repository.
- The session id, which the exit summary prints. `/resume` also lists them.

### Read it in the session

```text
/usage
/context
/usage health
```

`/usage` covers session usage and supported subscription quotas. `/context` shows context use and the newest call's cache evidence. `/usage health` shows process health and route state.

### Read it from the shell

```sh
clio-coder telemetry inspect <session>
clio-coder telemetry cost <session> --by model
clio-coder telemetry calls <session> --limit 20
clio-coder telemetry cache <session>
```

Each takes `--json` and returns the same data the terminal, editors, and desktop app read. For a repository over time, use `clio-coder telemetry cost --repo . --days 30 --by model`.

### Ask why it stopped

```sh
clio-coder telemetry why-stopped <session>
clio-coder telemetry timeline <session>
clio-coder telemetry explain <ref>
```

`explain` shows how a figure was derived. `--run <run-id>` points `inspect` and `cost` at one worker run instead of a session.

### Check a record

```sh
clio-coder telemetry verify <session>
clio-coder telemetry verify --run <run-id>
```

A sealed scope directory is self-contained, so you can copy it and verify it on another machine. `verify` checks journal segments, objects, and seals.

### Share it deliberately

```sh
clio-coder telemetry share --session <id> --profile content-free --dry-run
clio-coder telemetry share --session <id> --profile content-free --out report.tar.gz
```

Without `--send`, `share` writes an archive and uploads nothing. `content-free` is the default profile, with structural records and no objects or content. `structural` adds objects that hold structure, such as prompt manifests. Read the dry run before you send anything.

![Terminal output: telemetry why-stopped shows a closed session with spend not measured, telemetry verify reports the session sealed with 66 lines in one segment, and telemetry cost by turn shows tokens as lower bounds and cost as not measured.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/cli-telemetry-session.webp)

*A gateway that reports no usage: token figures are lower bounds, cost reads not measured, and the record still verifies.*

**What you should see**

Figures labelled by provenance, and a `verify` result that names any gap. A clean verify shows the journals are internally consistent. The chain is unsigned, so it does not show who wrote them, and it says nothing about whether the work was correct.

## Control what is kept

`telemetry.mode` defaults to `standard`, which keeps accountability and operational records without prompt content. `research` mode, `telemetry.research.content: true`, and `clio-coder telemetry consent` for the workspace are all required before prompts and request bodies are kept. Consent is stored in your own state directory, keyed by the workspace's real path, so a file committed to a repository cannot grant it.

`clio-coder telemetry prune` is a dry run unless you pass `--apply`.

**Boundaries**

- Figures depend on what the provider reports. Calls with unknown usage are counted separately.
- Quota rows are what a provider account reports, shared across sessions, and are separate from session spend.
- `clio-coder usage report` is experimental.

**Next steps**

- [Keep a long coding task on track](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/keep-long-coding-tasks-on-track.html)
- [Run it unattended within limits](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/run-it-unattended-within-limits.html)
- [Check your installation](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/doctor.html)

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/temperature-calibration.html

# A numerical change, checked with CLIO Coder

> Follow a temperature-conversion example through a floating-point test failure, a correction, and recorded verification.

A small numerical task makes it easy to follow a change from code to a recorded check. This example converts temperatures between Celsius, Kelvin, and Fahrenheit, validates inputs, and tests physical boundaries without adding dependencies.

## Before you start

- CLIO Coder installed, with a connected model that supports tool calling.
- Node.js 18.1 or newer and npm on your `PATH`. The installer's private Node.js is not added to `PATH`, so install them yourself.
- The example archive below, extracted into a project you can open.

## Open the example

Download the [runnable temperature-calibration example](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/temperature-calibration.zip). It includes the actual implementation, seven tests, and a private package manifest. It uses only the built-in Node.js test runner and has no dependencies.

Extract the archive into your project's `examples/` folder, so the files live in `examples/temperature-calibration/`. Open the project in the terminal:

```sh
clio-coder
```

Select a model that supports tool calling. You can also use the desktop alpha with `clio-coder gui --open`. To reproduce the authoring task in your own project, ask:

> Create four temperature conversion functions for Celsius, Kelvin, and Fahrenheit. Reject non-numeric and non-finite inputs with TypeError, and temperatures below absolute zero with RangeError. Use 273.15 for the Celsius/Kelvin offset. Add Node.js tests for freezing, boiling, absolute zero, round trips within 1e-10, and invalid inputs. Use no dependencies. Run the tests and report the actual result.

Choose a new example directory when creating files. In the supplied example, the implementation and tests are already present; start by asking CLIO Coder to read them.

## Check the numerical boundaries

These reference temperatures cover ordinary values and the physical lower boundary:

| Reference | Celsius | Kelvin | Fahrenheit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Freezing point | 0 °C | 273.15 K | 32 °F |
| Boiling point | 100 °C | 373.15 K | 212 °F |
| Absolute zero | −273.15 °C | 0 K | −459.67 °F |

When CLIO Coder first wrote this example, the first run exposed an exact-equality assertion for the Fahrenheit value at absolute zero. JavaScript produced `−459.66999999999996`; the test expected `−459.67`. The agent changed that assertion to an absolute tolerance of `1e-10` and reran the tests. Review a tolerance against your domain’s numerical requirements before applying it elsewhere.

## Run a declared check

The example’s private `package.json` declares its test command. With the archive extracted into the folder above, ask CLIO Coder:

> Use verify with check test and cwd examples/temperature-calibration, then show the reference temperatures from examples/temperature-calibration/calibration.test.mjs as a table. Do not edit files.

If an approval card appears, read the command before allowing it. In the recorded run, the check exited 0 with seven passing tests, and CLIO Coder read the test file for the table. Naming the file keeps a fast model from searching the project for it.

![CLIO Coder in the terminal running the declared test check through verify with exit 0, then showing the reference temperatures from the test file as a table](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/tui-verify-table.webp)

To run the same tests yourself from the repository root:

```sh
node --test examples/temperature-calibration/calibration.test.mjs
```

## Inspect the recorded result

In the terminal, open `/view` and select the `checked test` row. The preview shows the check, its working directory, the exit status, and the output, so you can compare the answer with what ran. On the desktop alpha, **Artifacts** in the Session column lists the same record.

![Terminal View dock with the session's records on the left and the checked test row selected; the preview shows check test, its working directory examples/temperature-calibration, exit 0, the test command, and the passing test lines.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/tui-view-result.webp)

*/view: the recorded check, with its working directory, exit status and output.*

Passing tests establish the behavior covered by those tests. This small example does not establish the scientific validity of a larger application. For project-specific requirements, see [quality policies](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/quality-policy.html) and [tool usage](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/tool-usage.html).

**Next steps**

- [Submit a Slurm job through CLIO Coder](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/submit-a-slurm-job.html)
- [Check a change against your repository](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/check-a-change-against-your-repository.html)
- [Quality policy guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/quality-policy.html)
