Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/run-on-a-local-model.html

# Run CLIO Coder on a local model

> Connect a local server with no account or key, check what CLIO Coder learned about it, and see what else to check if code must stay on your machine.

You can run CLIO Coder with a model on your own machine, with no account and no API key. This guide connects a local server, checks what CLIO Coder learned about it, and shows what else to look at if your code must not leave the machine.

**Version scope**

This guide describes v0.8.0. Supported local servers include Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, vLLM, SGLang, and Lemonade. Whether a given model handles long agentic work is yours to test, and setup does not test it for you.

## Before you start

- A local server running, with a model that supports tool calling loaded.
- CLIO Coder installed, and a repository you know.

## Connect it

```sh
cd /path/to/your/project
clio-coder configure
```

Choose **Guided setup**. A server already running on a default local port is listed first, under **Clio found a way to reach a model**. Otherwise choose **A model server or gateway** and enter its address, or choose **Connect by endpoint** when you already know the URL. LM Studio commonly serves at `http://localhost:1234`, and Ollama at `http://localhost:11434`.

Setup may pick the model for you: a detected server comes with the first model it lists. Use `/model` afterwards to choose one that supports tool calling. Setup checks that the server is reachable, reads its model list, and sends one short test request before saving. It does not test tool calling, so the first real test comes next.

## Check what CLIO Coder learned

```sh
clio-coder targets --json
clio-coder doctor
```

In `targets --json`, `contextWindowProvenance` says where the window figure came from, such as a value the server reported or one you configured. A local server has no fallback number. If a figure looks wrong, set `targets[].capabilities.contextWindow`, or `ollama.numCtx` for Ollama, which is sent with every request.

## Ask something you can check

**Example**

> Read the build configuration and name the command that runs the tests. Run it and report the result. Do not edit files.

**What you should see**

Tool calls that really run, followed by an answer that matches your project. If the model writes out a command as text and never calls a tool, this model or server is not handling tool calls correctly, so try another before going further.

![Terminal transcript in which Qwopus3.8 runs ls, reads package.json, and runs npm test with exit 0, then names npm test as the test command and reports one test passed and none failed.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/tui-local-model-tools.webp)

*Tool calls that really ran on a self-hosted model reached through a LiteLLM gateway, then an answer that matches the project.*

## Keep the work on your machine

A local chat route does not by itself make the whole session local.

- Memory uses the chat route when no memory connection is set, so it stays local unless you name another. Compaction does the same unless `context.compaction.model` names another.
- System One is off by default. A hosted route would send data out.
- Web tools, MCP servers, plugins, peers, and shell commands can still make network requests.

To enforce a boundary for named files, use [information-flow rules](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/information-flow-rules.html).

**Boundaries**

- Local inference costs no provider fee, though hardware and power still cost money. `clio-coder usage report` shows these calls as free.
- Local servers vary in how they handle tool calls, cache, and long context. Expect to try more than one model.
- Automatic discovery at startup checks default ports only, takes the first model listed, and uses a server it finds only after you say yes. Set a route with `clio-coder configure` to choose one.

**Next steps**

- [Choose a model for your project](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/choose-model-for-your-project.html)
- [Connection guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html)
- [When do several agents or small models pay off?](https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/fleets-and-local-models.html)

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/submit-a-slurm-job.html

# Submit a Slurm job through CLIO Coder

> Declare the clio-kit Slurm server, install the skill, and let the agent submit and follow a job, with a confirmation before it reaches the scheduler.

CLIO Coder can submit and follow a Slurm job for you through the clio-kit MCP server. Each submission or cancellation is confirmed first: the safety judge reviews it against your own messages, and you decide when it has no verdict. Use this when a task needs real compute and you want the job's outcome reported back into the session.

**Version scope**

This guide describes v0.8.0. CLIO Coder has no scheduler tier of its own: the agent calls the server's tools, and Slurm does the rest. Fleet workers do not submit through Slurm.

## Before you start

- A host where `sbatch`, `squeue`, `scontrol`, and `scancel` reach your cluster.
- An interactive session. A headless run submits only when the safety judge allows it.
- A job script you are willing to run under your allocation.

## Install the server

```sh
uv tool install clio-kit
clio-kit mcp-server slurm
```

The second command lets clio-kit prepare its private runtime, which can take longer than the 15 seconds CLIO Coder allows a server to start on a first launch. Stop it with Ctrl-C once it is running.

## Declare it

Run `clio-coder paths` to find your config directory, then add this as `mcp.yaml` there:

```yaml title=mcp.yaml
version: 1
servers:
  - id: slurm
    command: clio-kit
    args: [mcp-server, slurm]
    timeoutMs: 120000
```

Keep the id `slurm`. The `slurm-jobs` skill you install below expects it, and it is what switches on the confirmation for allocations.

```sh
clio-coder doctor --verbose
clio-coder mcp list --refresh
```

Until the first refresh, plain `mcp list` shows the declaration with no recorded tool catalog. `--refresh` starts each trusted server, lists its tools live, and records the catalog.

Plain `doctor` folds the Slurm checks into one row while none of them needs attention:

```text
OK   slurm                  ready: clio-kit, mcp server, scheduler
INFO scheduler commands     sbatch is on PATH: scheduler commands run outside the shell sandbox with approval
```

`doctor --verbose` prints the `slurm clio-kit`, `slurm mcp server` and `slurm scheduler` rows separately, and a row with a warning always keeps its own line.

The server row names the `mcp.yaml` that declares it and its trust. The scheduler row means only that `sbatch` and `squeue` answered `--version`; it does not contact the controller. None of these rows fails the check.

The host in the picture below has no Slurm client, so its scheduler row reads `INFO slurm scheduler        sbatch not on PATH; squeue not on PATH`. The two rows above are what a host with the clients prints.

![Terminal: doctor --verbose filtered to its Slurm rows reports sbatch not on PATH, clio-kit OK with the slurm server, the slurm MCP server OK as declared and trusted in the user mcp.yaml, and the scheduler as INFO because sbatch and squeue are not on PATH; mcp list shows the server with no recorded tool catalog, and mcp list --refresh lists its five tools: submit and cancel as execute, list, describe and cluster as read.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/cli-slurm-doctor.webp)

*The setup checks on a host with no scheduler: the server is declared and trusted, its tools are listed, and doctor reports sbatch and squeue missing.*

## Install the skill

```sh
clio-coder library install skill:slurm-jobs --project --dry-run
clio-coder library install skill:slurm-jobs --project
```

## Submit one job

**Example**

> /skill slurm-jobs Run scripts/smoke.sbatch on the debug partition with 2 cores for 5 minutes. Report the exit code and the last lines of stdout.

The skill checks that the server is declared, looks at the partition, and submits once. The submission is confirmed before the job reaches the scheduler. When the safety judge has no verdict, an approval card appears, so read the script, cores, memory, and time limit before you press Enter.

The skill then polls with a growing wait until the job reaches a terminal state, and fetches bounded output.

**What you should see**

The answer ends with a line in this form: `Slurm job <id>: <state>, exit <code>, stdout <path>, stderr <path>`. Check that job id against `squeue` or `sacct` if the result matters.

To keep a job's output beside its record rather than in scratch space, ask the agent to put it into the project store, or run `clio-coder store put results <stdout path> --note "Slurm job <id>"` yourself. The store lives on the host where CLIO Coder runs, here the login node, and records where each file came from.

## Without the server

The agent can also run `sbatch`, `squeue`, `scancel` and the other Slurm, PBS, LSF and Flux clients through `bash`. They run outside the shell sandbox, because they reach the scheduler through a host daemon the sandbox blocks, and they get the same review as `ssh`.

At `default` the safety judge decides first and asks you when it has no verdict. Contained `yolo` runs one only when your own message names it, and unconfined `yolo` runs it.

A script that calls `sbatch` itself stays inside the sandbox and fails there, and so does a workspace file named like a client, such as `./sbatch`. Submit from the command line the agent runs, not from a wrapper. With `safety.sandbox: required` at unconfined `yolo`, only a one-line `sbatch`, `squeue`, `scancel`, `sacct` or `sinfo` with listed options leaves the sandbox; `srun`, `salloc` and `flux` stay inside.

## Cancel a job

Ask the agent to cancel the job by id. Cancelling is confirmed the same way, and the server refuses unless the job id is repeated exactly.

**Boundaries**

- In a headless `clio-coder run` at `default`, a submission or cancellation runs only when the safety judge allows it. With no verdict it is denied.
- At `default`, a trust setting cannot make a submission skip the confirmation, which is attached to the tool name.
- Your site's allocation rules and data policies still apply. A login node is not a compute node.
- This repository ships no copy of the server's schema, so the installed clio-kit version is the authority on tool parameters.

**Next steps**

- [Run a research campaign and a blind arena](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/run-a-research-campaign-and-a-blind-arena.html)
- [Pre-register a benchmark before you measure](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/pre-register-a-benchmark.html)
- [Slurm workflows](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/slurm.html)
- [Install on a cluster](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/hpc-clusters.html)
- [What would make a scientist trust an agent's change?](https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/scientific-and-hpc-workflows.html)

# Pre-register a benchmark before you measure

> Use the experiment-protocol skill to lock thresholds, tolerances, and verdict conditions into a contract you commit before any result exists.

A benchmark is easy to fool once you have seen the result. The `experiment-protocol` skill has CLIO Coder write down the outcome, thresholds, tolerances, and verdict conditions before any measurement, and then keep to them. Use it for a performance study, a numerical comparison, a parameter sweep, or a solver comparison.

**Version scope**

This guide describes v0.8.0 and skill version 0.3.3. To find out why one output is wrong, use `scientific-debugging` instead, since that is a diagnosis and not an experiment.

## Before you start

- A repository with the code to measure and input data you can checksum.
- A chat route, in the terminal or a headless run.
- An environment you can pin: compiler, flags, package versions, and node class.

## Install the skill

```sh
clio-coder library install skill:experiment-protocol --project --dry-run
clio-coder library install skill:experiment-protocol --project
```

Read the dry run first. It shows the destination and the pin.

## Ask for a pre-registration

**Example**

> /skill experiment-protocol Compare the new solver against the current one on data/mesh-256.h5 for step time and accuracy. Stop after you write the contract so I can review it.

The contract goes in `.clio-coder/validation.yaml`, or `VALIDATION.md` at the repository root. A YAML contract that parses raises the repository's rigor to high, so a claim that the work is done must carry validation evidence or state a limitation. `VALIDATION.md` is read as advice and does not raise rigor.

## Review the contract

This is the step that matters, and it is yours. Check that the contract has each of these:

- **Outcome**: one sentence, with a number.
- **Thresholds**: a minimum below which the result is refuted, a target, and a stretch.
- **Tolerances**: absolute or relative, stated per metric. A bare `1e-6` is not a tolerance.
- **Environment pin**: compiler and flags, versions, node class, and scheduler context.
- **Input identity**: paths with checksums.
- **Verdict conditions**: what makes the result confirmed, refuted, or inconclusive.

Commit it before measuring anything, so the history shows it came first. In a headless run nobody can answer questions, so the skill records unstated details as explicit assumptions. Read those assumptions closely.

## Run it

The skill captures a baseline under the pinned environment, then changes one independent variable per run, and records job ids and node lists where a scheduler is involved. It compares results against the registered thresholds only.

**What you should see**

A verdict of confirmed, refuted, or inconclusive against the numbers you committed, with any deviation logged next to the result. Rejected approaches go in a dead-ends ledger. A refuted result plus a ledger entry is a successful experiment.

## Let a research campaign search under the contract

The contract's validators are prose until the project declares matching checks. Write them as checks in `.clio-coder/verifiers.yaml`, here a `bench` check whose command prints `{"step_ms": ...}` and an `accuracy` check of kind `numeric-compare` with the registered tolerance, and commit the file.

A `research` campaign can then search for improvements without moving the goalposts:

```sh
clio-coder research start --check bench --metric step_ms --direction min \
  --gate accuracy --max-iterations 5 --scope "src/solver/**" \
  --goal "reduce step time without changing any answer beyond the registered tolerance"
```

It first measures the base against itself and stops if that alone looks like a change, unless you pass `--allow-noisy`.

A candidate is kept only when the median improves by at least 5% (the default) with a 95% interval that excludes zero, and when every `--gate` check passes. A candidate that edits the check file or any file a check names is discarded unmeasured, so the thresholds you committed stay the ones that judge it.

**Boundaries**

- Watch for a threshold or tolerance edited after results appeared. The skill treats that as a red flag, and `git log` on the contract shows it.
- A single run on a shared machine does not establish a claim. Size repetitions to the noise.
- Findings outside the registered outcome are exploratory and need their own pre-registration.
- The skill checks process. Whether the tolerance is scientifically right is a judgment for someone who knows the field.

**Next steps**

- [Work from a laptop with remote workers](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/work-from-a-laptop-with-remote-workers.html)
- [Run a research campaign and a blind arena](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/run-a-research-campaign-and-a-blind-arena.html)
- [Check a change against your repository](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/check-a-change-against-your-repository.html)
- [Research campaigns and arena](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/research-and-arena.html)
- [What would make a scientist trust an agent's change?](https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/scientific-and-hpc-workflows.html)

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/keep-results-in-the-project-store.html

# Keep results outside the tree with the project store

> Store a result with a note, check it for drift, read it from a script, and let a worker write into one granted tag.

Results, datasets and checkpoints do not belong in Git, but scattering them across scratch folders loses track of where each came from. The project store keeps them outside the working tree, in named tags, with a record of what produced each file and whether it has changed since. You, the agent and its workers all see the same store.

**Version scope**

This tutorial describes v0.8.0 and the store's default local backend. The output below is from the `clio-coder store` command run on Linux, where the store has been exercised.

## Before you start

- CLIO Coder installed, and a project in a Git repository.
- A result file to keep, here `run-042.csv`.

## Put a result in the store

From the project folder:

```sh
clio-coder store put results run-042.csv --note "baseline, 64 ranks"
```

**What you should see**

`stored results:run-042.csv (8 B) from /home/alice/proj/run-042.csv`. The `results` tag did not exist, so the put created it.

A tag is a named container and a blob is a file in it; `results:run-042.csv` names one blob. List what you have with `clio-coder store tags` and `clio-coder store ls results`. `clio-coder store where` prints the folder the store lives in, under CLIO Coder's data directory, so it does not count against the repository and every checkout and task worktree of the project shares it.

## Check whether it changed

```sh
clio-coder store stat results:run-042.csv
```

**What you should see**

A `ref`, `path`, `bytes` and `sha256` line, and `drift     none`. Drift is `none` while the blob matches its record, `changed` when its bytes no longer match, `missing` when it is gone, and `unrecorded` when there is no record for it.

To check a whole tag at once, run `clio-coder store verify results`. It prints a count for each state, names any blob that is not `ok`, and exits 1 unless every blob is `ok`, so a job script can stop on it.

`clio-coder store history results:run-042.csv` lists every put, note and removal, with its hash, its source file and its note. The history is write-once.

## Read it from a script

`store get` prints the path of a read-only copy, so a script reads the stored bytes without any chance of changing them:

```sh
python3 analyze.py "$(clio-coder store get results:run-042.csv)"
```

Use `--to <path>` to copy the blob somewhere instead. In a session, ask for the same thing in words:

**Example**

> Plot the y column of results:run-042.csv against x and save the figure as fig-042.png. Put the figure in the results tag with a note naming the input.

The agent reaches the store through its `store` tool, and reading needs no approval.

When the figure comes from a script the agent ran with its `run_script` tool, the stored record keeps the script's hash and its declared inputs, and an input that came from the store is named by its `<tag>:<blob>`. Notes can be added later, and `derived_from` records which blobs a result was made from.

## Let a worker write results

A dispatched worker reads the store but does not write it unless its dispatch grants it tags. Ask for the grant by name:

**Example**

> Hand this to a researcher worker: rerun the analysis for runs 043 to 045 and put each figure in the results tag. Grant it the results tag only.

The tag must exist before the dispatch. The worker may then `put` and `note` into `results` and nowhere else in the store. A read-only run, an ACP agent or a worker on a remote node cannot be granted tags.

## Replace and remove with care

The store keeps no earlier versions of a blob, and no workspace snapshot covers it.

When the agent would replace a blob or remove one, it asks you first and names the blob. From the shell, `clio-coder store put` over an existing blob replaces it and says `replaced`. `clio-coder store rm results:run-042.csv` only prints what it would delete; add `--yes` to delete it. The blob's records remain.

**Boundaries**

- The local backend lives on one host. A worker on another node through an SSH fleet sees that node's own store.
- `put` copies bytes. A large dataset takes its size again in the store.
- Above 64 MiB the record omits the hash; `clio-coder store verify results --hash-large` hashes such blobs and records the digest as a note.
- `clio-coder reset --data`, `reset --all`, and `uninstall` without `--keep-data` delete the store, and nothing recovers it.
- The clio-core backend is experimental in v0.8.0.

**Next steps**

- [Keep results in the store](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/store.html)
- [The store tool and its limits](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/tool-usage.html)
- [Workers and fleets](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/fleet-dispatch.html)
- [Submit a Slurm job](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/submit-a-slurm-job.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/set-up-a-lab-from-one-setup-file.html

# Set up a lab from one setup file

> Write one YAML file that connects every lab member to your model gateway, check what it may carry, and test the route.

A lab or site that runs its own model gateway can connect every member's CLIO Coder with one small YAML file. You publish it once; each member imports it, sees where their prompts will go, and confirms. The file can name models and where to find a key, but it can never carry a key or change what CLIO Coder is allowed to do.

**Version scope**

This tutorial describes v0.8.0. The output below is from `clio-coder configure --import` run against a fresh CLIO Coder home.

## Before you start

- An OpenAI-compatible model gateway your members can reach, here `https://llm.lab.example.org/v1`.
- A way to give each member a key, which they keep in an environment variable.
- An `https` address or a shared path where you can publish the file.

## Write the setup file

```yaml title=lab-clio.yaml
notes: "Lab gateway. Ask #research-computing for a key; export it as LAB_API_KEY."
targets:
  - id: lab
    runtime: openai-compat
    url: https://llm.lab.example.org/v1
    defaultModel: qwen3-coder-480b
    capabilities: { contextWindow: 131072 }
    auth: { apiKeyEnvVar: LAB_API_KEY }
chat: { target: lab }
fleet: { target: lab, model: qwen3-coder-480b }
```

`targets` lists the model endpoints. `chat` and `fleet` choose which target the main session and its workers use. `notes` is shown to the member before they confirm, so use it to say how to get a key.

## Know what the file may carry

A setup file may hold only `targets`, `chat`, `fleet` and `notes`. A target may hold only `id`, `runtime`, `url`, `defaultModel`, `wireModels`, `capabilities`, `pricing` and `auth`, and `auth` only names an environment variable (`apiKeyEnvVar`) or an OAuth profile. Anything else refuses the whole file. A literal key is the usual mistake:

```yaml title=bad.yaml
targets:
  - id: lab2
    runtime: openai-compat
    url: https://x/v1
    auth: { apiKey: sk-123 }
```

**What you should see**

`error: setup file refused; nothing changed:` followed by `targets[0].auth.apiKey is not allowed in a setup file`, and exit code 1.

The same rule refuses request headers and safety settings, so a member never has to read a setup file for hidden permissions.

## Try it on your own account first

```sh
clio-coder configure --import lab-clio.yaml
```

**What you should see**

```text
Setup file lab-clio.yaml will:
Lab gateway. Ask #research-computing for a key; export it as LAB_API_KEY.

  add target lab (openai-compat)
    prompts go to https://llm.lab.example.org/v1
    model qwen3-coder-480b; key from $LAB_API_KEY
  chat uses lab / qwen3-coder-480b
  fleet uses lab / qwen3-coder-480b
Apply these changes? [y/N]
```

Answer `n` and nothing changes. Answer `y` and it prints `Imported 1 target.` and one line per target: `lab: ready`, or what is still missing, such as `lab reads its key from LAB_API_KEY, which is not set in this shell.`

A plain `http` address to anything other than this machine or a private network address adds a warning that prompts and keys cross the network unencrypted.

Importing saves the settings without sending a request to the model. Check the route yourself:

```sh
export LAB_API_KEY=...
clio-coder doctor
clio-coder targets --probe --target lab
```

The `chat` row of `doctor` should end in `endpoint reachable`, and the probe's `health` column should not read `down`.

## Publish it

Put the file at an `https` address or a path members can read. A fetched file must be `https` all the way, a redirect to anything else is refused, and the file may be at most 64 KiB.

## What a member sees

A member who has never run CLIO Coder runs `clio-coder`. At **What do you have?** they choose **A setup file from my lab or team**, type the address at **Where is the setup file?**, and see the same preview under **This setup file will:** with **Apply** and **Back**. A member who already uses CLIO Coder runs:

```sh
clio-coder configure --import https://lab.example.org/clio-coder/setup.yaml
```

Only the `lab` target and the chat and fleet routes change. Their other targets, project settings and stored keys stay as they were.

Importing the same file again prints `Setup file already imported; nothing changed` with the status line, so it is safe to put in a login script with `--yes`. Without a terminal and without `--yes`, the command prints the preview and exits 2 without saving.

## Change the file later

If you change the settings of a target a member already has, their import is refused with `lab already saved with different settings; nothing changed.` and the command to rerun with `--replace`. Tell members when you change it. A new target id imports without `--replace`.

**Boundaries**

- Importing does not test the model. Members should run `clio-coder doctor` after setting their key.
- The file cannot hand out keys. Each member still gets a key and exports it in their shell.
- A member can change their route afterwards with `/model` or `clio-coder configure`; the file is not enforced.

**Next steps**

- [Connect CLIO Coder on an HPC login node](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/hpc-clusters.html)
- [Setup files and model targets](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html)
- [Run on a local model](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/run-on-a-local-model.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/share-a-folder-with-a-teammate-or-a-second-terminal.html

# Share a folder with a teammate or a second terminal

> Run two sessions in one project, keep each person's state private, and commit project settings that can only make CLIO Coder stricter.

Two people can work in one project folder with CLIO Coder, and so can you in two terminals. What they share is the folder: its files and the project settings committed under `.clio-coder/`. Each session, its transcript, its credentials and its approvals stay with the person who started it, and the project settings can make CLIO Coder stricter for everyone but never looser.

**Version scope**

This tutorial describes v0.8.0. The output below is from CLIO Coder run against a fresh CLIO Coder home and a new Git repository; paths are shortened to the default layout.

## Before you start

- CLIO Coder installed for each person, in their own account.
- A project folder each of you can open: a shared filesystem, or a clone of the same repository.

## Open a second terminal

Run `clio-coder` in the folder from a second terminal while the first is still open. The second launch never joins the first one's session. It prints:

```text
Clio Coder: this folder already has a Clio in another terminal; this one has its own panes.
```

It then starts its own private pane host, with its own session and its own docks. A folder can have up to four pane hosts at once. A fifth terminal runs without panes, still with its own session, until one of the four exits.

The two sessions see each other's work only as changed files on disk. Give each one a different part of the tree, and read `git diff` before you commit what either produced.

## Keep your state yours

Each person's sessions, transcripts and approvals live in their own CLIO Coder home, never in the project. `clio-coder paths` shows where:

```text
config   /home/you/.config/clio-coder
data     /home/you/.local/share/clio-coder
state    /home/you/.local/state/clio-coder
cache    /home/you/.cache/clio-coder
project  /home/you/lab-model
```

These directories are created owner-only (`0700`), and session transcripts are under `state/sessions`. On a shared machine, keep `CLIO_CODER_HOME` and the state directory out of shared project space. If a state directory is open to other users, `clio-coder doctor` says so:

```text
WARN state dir mode         /home/you/.local/state/clio-coder is 755: group or other users can enter it and read session transcripts (run `clio-coder doctor --fix`, or `chmod 700` it when the directory is not Clio's alone)
```

`clio-coder doctor --fix` closes it and reports `tightened to 700`.

## Commit project settings that only tighten

`.clio-coder/settings.yaml` holds settings for everyone who opens the folder. Here a project lowers the session spending ceiling and tries to loosen two other controls:

```yaml title=.clio-coder/settings.yaml
version: 2
safety:
  autonomy: yolo
  limits:
    sessionCostUsd: 2
    chatToolCallsPerTurn: 200
```

Nobody's CLIO Coder reads this file until that person approves it. Run `clio-coder config trust settings` to see the captured bytes and the command that approves exactly those bytes:

```text
Review the captured files above. Approve exactly these bytes with:
clio-coder config trust settings --hash 8917fe3bce74889bee87a978044311d803678e1ae96dbd6f19d3af95c796a061
```

After the approval, `clio-coder config inspect` shows what the project actually changed:

```text
! settings project: /home/you/lab-model/.clio-coder/settings.yaml: safety.autonomy: project autonomy may only tighten the level in user settings; project value ignored
! settings project: /home/you/lab-model/.clio-coder/settings.yaml: safety.limits.chatToolCallsPerTurn: a project may only tighten a limit from user settings; project value ignored
safety.limits.sessionCostUsd = 2  [project]
```

The lower spending ceiling applies. `yolo` and the higher tool-call limit were dropped, because the user's own settings allow less. A project can tighten `yolo` to `default`, never the reverse, and the same rule covers the sandbox, snapshots, worker permissions and every safety and fleet limit.

**What the approval covers**

The approval is yours, for this folder and these bytes. It is stored in your config directory, so a teammate approves the same file separately. If the file changes, CLIO Coder ignores it again until each of you reviews the new bytes.

## Keep personal overrides out of Git

`.clio-coder/settings.local.yaml` is a second project layer for overrides of your own. The first time CLIO Coder generates a file in `.clio-coder/`, it writes an allow-list `.clio-coder/.gitignore` that keeps `*.local.yaml` and generated files out of Git while authored settings, skills and rules can be committed.

Project layers never carry credentials. Keys such as `auth`, `apiKey`, `token`, `secret` and `password` are dropped with a diagnostic, and a project target that points at a URL is never sent your stored or environment keys. Each person keeps their key in their own settings or credential store.

**Boundaries**

- Approval is per person, per surface and per folder. Approving settings does not approve the project's hooks, safety rules, extensions or plugins.
- Two sessions in one folder do not coordinate their edits. Split the work, and review the diff before committing.
- A pane host per terminal is verified on Linux only.

**Next steps**

- [Settings layers and project trust](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html)
- [Panes and the pane host](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/panes-and-files.html)
- [Connect CLIO Coder on an HPC login node](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/hpc-clusters.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/run-a-research-campaign-and-a-blind-arena.html

# Run a research campaign and a blind arena

> Keep a speed-up only when a measurement proves it and the answers still match, then compare model answers without knowing which model wrote them.

You changed some code and it feels faster, or one model's answer looks better than another's. CLIO Coder has two commands that replace that impression with a record. `clio-coder research` keeps a change only when a measurement shows a real gain and every correctness check still passes. `clio-coder arena` shows you answers from several models without their names, and records your vote.

**Version scope**

This guide describes v0.8.0. The output below comes from one recorded session with a single model, Qwen 3.8 27B, on a small Python project. One model is enough to learn both commands. It is not enough to rank models, and the arena section shows why.

## Before you start

- CLIO Coder installed, with a connected model.
- A Git repository with a check that prints a number as JSON, and a second check that proves the answers are still right.
- Whatever the checks need installed before you start. The agent cannot install it during the campaign.

## Declare what to measure and what must not break

The project here has a `summary()` function that returns a mean, a median and a variance. It is correct and slow. `bench.py` times it on 3000 values and prints `{"wall_ms": ...}`. `check.py` prints the answers for a holdout input, and `tests/reference/stats.json` holds the expected values.

```yaml title=.clio-coder/verifiers.yaml
version: 2
checks:
  - id: bench
    description: Wall time of summary() on 3000 values (min is better)
    tags: [perf]
    kind: command
    command: [python3, bench.py]
    cwd: .
    timeoutMs: 60000
  - id: correct
    description: summary() answers match the reference on a holdout input
    tags: [correctness]
    kind: numeric-compare
    command: [python3, check.py]
    reference: tests/reference/stats.json
    tolerance: { relative: 1.0e-9 }
    cwd: .
    timeoutMs: 60000
```

Every check needs `id`, `description`, `command`, `cwd`, `timeoutMs` and `tags`; an empty `tags: []` is allowed. Commit the catalog and every file the checks run or name. Each campaign worktree starts from `HEAD`, so an uncommitted `bench.py` or reference file is not there.

The tolerance is your definition of the same answer. Here, a relative difference up to one part in a billion still passes.

## Run a short campaign

```sh
clio-coder research start --check bench --metric wall_ms --direction min \
  --max-iterations 2 --gate correct --scope stats.py --max-wall-minutes 25 \
  --goal "make stats.py faster without changing any answer"
```

`--scope` limits which files the agent may change, and an iteration that changes anything outside it is archived without being measured. The checks and every file they name are protected the same way, so the agent cannot speed up the benchmark by editing it.

**What the recorded session printed**

```text
campaign r20261112-192812-1d5d (stopped: max-iterations)
objective: min wall_ms from check bench; min improvement +5.00%, 5 pairs
gates: correct; scope: stats.py
protected: .clio-coder/verifiers.yaml, bench.py, check.py, tests/reference/stats.json
agent: autonomy default
branch: clio/research/r20261112-192812-1d5d at 37407c7dee9e (base 39930e6fbfbf, 2 ratchets)
budget: 2/2 iterations, 25 min wall; spend not measured; 2 run(s) had unknown spend
A/A: quiet; unchanged, median delta +4.04%, 95% CI [-0.96%, +6.93%]
  it-0001  ratcheted; improved, median delta -99.74%, 95% CI [-99.76%, -99.71%]; gates correct pass; cost unknown
  it-0002  ratcheted; improved, median delta -17.69%, 95% CI [-27.80%, -12.04%]; gates correct pass; cost unknown
stopped: max-iterations: ran 2 of 2 iterations
```

## Read the result line by line

Start with the A/A line. Before any change, CLIO Coder timed the unchanged code against itself in five interleaved pairs. The medians moved 4.04%, and the 95% interval spans zero, so the noise stayed under the 5% threshold. If the base against itself already looked like a change, the campaign would have stopped there unless you passed `--allow-noisy`.

Each iteration counts as improved only when the median moves at least 5% the right way and the bootstrap interval excludes zero. The first iteration removed almost all the time. The second found a further 17.69%, a gain that would be invisible by eye. Both passed the `correct` gate.

`spend not measured` is honest. This model was reached through a gateway with no price, so CLIO Coder cannot know what the runs cost, and it does not count unknown spend as zero. With `--max-cost-usd` on such a route, the campaign stops as `budget-unenforceable` unless you also pass `--allow-unpriced`.

## Audit it and take the change

```sh
clio-coder research report r20261112-192812-1d5d
git diff HEAD clio/research/r20261112-192812-1d5d
```

`report` regrades the A/A check and every iteration from the stored samples with the recorded seed. In the recorded session each line ended `agrees with the journal`, and the command exited 0. It exits 1 when a grade disagrees.

The result lives on the branch `clio/research/<id>`, and your checkout is never touched. Here the branch replaced an insertion sort with `sorted()`, stopped `variance` from recomputing the mean for every element, and used `sum()` for the mean. Review the diff and merge it yourself.

## Compare answers blind

```sh
clio-coder arena run --suite speed --check correct \
  --contender litellm/qwen3.8-27b --contender litellm/qwen3.8-27b \
  -- "Make summary() in stats.py faster without changing any answer. Keep the change minimal."
```

A contender is `<target>/<model>`. Each one runs as a normal `clio-coder run` in its own worktree from `HEAD`, and `--check` runs the named check on each result. Naming the same model twice is an A/A match: it shows how much two runs of one model differ before you read anything into a difference between two models.

To name your own contenders, `clio-coder targets` lists each target id with its model, a local server's target included.

| | Contender A | Contender B |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Change | One line: `variance` reuses the mean it already computed | Two edits: the same fix, and `sorted()` for the median |
| Diff | `+1 -1` | `+2 -7` |
| `correct` check | Pass, every answer bit-identical | Pass, every answer bit-identical |
| Its own timing claim | 155 ms to 69 ms | 176 ms to 0.465 ms |

One model, one prompt and one starting commit gave two different readings of "keep the change minimal". That spread is the noise any model comparison has to beat.

## Vote, then reveal

```sh
clio-coder arena show 20261112-193135-2727
clio-coder arena vote 20261112-193135-2727 B --note "both exact; B removes the quadratic sort too, still a small diff"
clio-coder arena show 20261112-193135-2727 --reveal
clio-coder arena standings --suite speed
```

Before a vote, `show` lists A and B in a seeded random order and hides the target, model, duration, tokens and cost. `--reveal` before a vote is refused. CLIO Coder never grades a contender; the vote is yours, and so is the note.

**What the recorded session printed**

```text
recorded B for match 20261112-193135-2727; arena show 20261112-193135-2727 reveals who is who
```

After the reveal, `standings` printed:

```text
no voted matches yet (1 recorded)
```

That is the inconclusive result, reported as it is. A match that pits a model against itself says nothing about the model, so standings skip it. To rank models, run matches with two or more different contenders. A rating appears once a model has 5 votes, and one vote is one person's judgment on one prompt.

**Boundaries**

- A campaign is only as good as its checks. A benchmark that measures the wrong thing will be optimized anyway.
- The `correct` gate checks one holdout input. Iteration answers that pass it can still differ elsewhere.
- Research runs one candidate per iteration and optimizes one number at a time.
- A single vote, and a single A/A match, are anecdotes. Standings mean something only after many matches with different contenders.

**Next steps**

- [Work from a laptop with remote workers](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/work-from-a-laptop-with-remote-workers.html)
- [Research campaigns and the arena](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/research-and-arena.html)
- [Check a change against your repository](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/check-a-change-against-your-repository.html)
- [Pre-register a benchmark](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/pre-register-a-benchmark.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/report-a-problem-without-leaking-your-machine.html

# Report a problem without leaking your machine

> Draft a bug report, read the exact text with your paths, names and keys masked, choose how it leaves, and share a diagnostic bundle only if you want to.

When CLIO Coder itself misbehaves, `/report` in a session and `clio-coder report` in a shell draft a bug report, a feature request or a question for its maintainers. You read the exact text before anything leaves your machine, with your paths, names and keys masked, and CLIO Coder never sends a report on its own. This tutorial previews a report and never sends one.

**Version scope**

This tutorial describes v0.8.0. The output below is from CLIO Coder run with `--dry-run` against a fresh CLIO Coder home and a small Git repository that had one finished session. Nothing was sent or saved.

## Before you start

- CLIO Coder installed.
- A folder where you have run at least one session, for `--last`.
- To send for real: the GitHub CLI `gh`, signed in. Without it you can still open or write the report.

## Draft a report

In a session, `/report bug footer flickers on resize` uses the summary as the title and adds what CLIO Coder observed in the current session. `/report feature` and `/report question` work the same way. From a shell, `--title` and `--body-file` supply the text, and `--last` adds the newest session in this folder:

```sh
clio-coder report bug --title "footer flickers on resize" --body-file notes.txt --last --dry-run
```

Without `--body-file`, a terminal opens `$EDITOR` on a template. `--session <id>` names another session. The note in this run named the machine and the project folder on purpose.

## Read what would be posted

The preview opens with where the report would go, then the body exactly as it would be sent:

```text
Public, posted from your gh account to github.com/iowarp/clio-coder; nothing sent yet

----- title -----

fix: footer flickers on resize

----- body, exactly as it will be sent -----
### What happened

The footer flickers when I resize the terminal on <host>.
Repro: open clio-coder in <path> and drag the window edge.
```

The host name and the folder were masked before the preview was shown. Below the body come an environment block (version, platform, Node, install kind and model) and a report block with an id. The preview ends with what was masked and what sending would do:

```text
Masked by Clio: 1 path, 1 host name. No secrets recognized.
No diagnostic bundle is attached.

Sending will, in this order:
  1. search iowarp/clio-coder for an existing report of the same problem
  2. post the text you reviewed as a public issue from your gh account
dry run: nothing sent
```

The masks cover local paths, URLs other than CLIO Coder's own, user, host, project, branch, remote and target names, e-mail and IP addresses, and secrets, including the API keys the process holds. The review then searches the text again for this machine's names, and refuses to send while one slipped past or the text holds hidden characters.

In the session, `e` edits the text in `$EDITOR` and masks the edit again, `m` masks or unmasks one value, Enter moves to the next step and Esc closes the review and keeps a draft.

## Choose how it leaves

What happens at the end depends on what the machine has:

- **Send.** With a signed-in `gh`, CLIO Coder searches GitHub for the same problem, then posts a public issue, or a discussion for a question, under your account. In a session only `s` on the send step sends, never Enter. In a shell you choose send at the prompt, or pass `--yes`.
- **Open.** Without `gh`, it opens a prefilled form in your browser, and you submit it there.
- **Write.** Without a browser, it writes the report to a file and prints the link to paste it into.
- **Preview.** `--dry-run` stops after the preview, with no network call.

The shell prompt can also save a draft for `clio-coder report send <id>` later. When the search finds an open report of the same problem, you choose to add your details to it, file a new issue that links it, or cancel. With `--yes`, `--on-duplicate stop` is the default: the draft is saved and the command exits 3.

## Attach a diagnostic bundle only if you want to

A bundle is opt-in and built only from a shell: add `--bundle mechanics --consent debug` with `--last` or `--session <id>`. Its preview lists what it keeps and what it never keeps:

```text
Never kept:
  - Prompts, model text, thinking, tool arguments and output, unless the transcript is ticked.
  - File contents, diffs, commit messages.
  - Absolute or relative paths, repository names and remotes, branch names.
  - Host and user names, endpoint URLs, target ids, agent, rule and hook names, environment variables.
  - Anything a schema does not bound.
```

`--transcript [N]` adds the last turns, scrubbed. `debug` lets the maintainers read the bundle to fix this report, and `dataset` also lets its mechanics go into public datasets. `clio-coder report selftest` builds the same bundle in memory and writes nothing. Here it printed `0 identifiers found in 11370 bytes`, and it exits 1 when an identifier survives.

Without `--share`, the bundle stays on your machine and the issue never carries it. `/report` in a session, over ACP or in the desktop app attaches no bundle.

## Share it encrypted, in your own account

`--share` encrypts the bundle so that only the maintainers' key opens it, and uploads it as a secret gist in your own GitHub account through your `gh`. The issue names the gist.

The preview in this run showed the pointer it would carry, `bundle: gist:<created on send>#shr_2784226036f4c9e7`: the gist is created only when you send, and deleted again if posting fails. Without a signed-in `gh`, the bundle is sealed to a `.box` file you attach by hand.

## Forget it later

`clio-coder report status` lists your reports and drafts, and `clio-coder report forget <id>` deletes a draft you never posted. A posted report cannot be withdrawn from CLIO Coder; edit or close it on GitHub. For a shared report, `forget` deletes the gist first, then offers a one-line comment asking the maintainers to delete their copy, posted only if you confirm.

Once a share is 180 days old, CLIO Coder deletes its gist the next time you run `clio-coder report` or `clio-coder telemetry share`. Nothing runs at startup or in the background. Your local copy of a sent report's bundle is deleted after 30 days.

**Exit codes**

`clio-coder report` exits 0 when the report was sent, opened in the browser, written or previewed; 1 when sending failed or a bundle was refused; 2 on a usage error, or outside a terminal without `--yes`; and 3 when a likely duplicate or a newer release stopped it and the draft was saved.

**Boundaries**

- The masks cover the names CLIO Coder knows about this machine. Text you typed about another machine can pass, so read the preview.
- A sent report is a public GitHub issue or discussion. Security problems never go there: `/report security` prints the link to the private advisory form.
- The agent can save a draft, but never send one or share a bundle. Only your own review sends.

**Next steps**

- [Report a problem to the maintainers](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/troubleshooting.html#report-a-problem-to-the-maintainers)
- [See what a session cost and what a run did](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/see-what-a-session-cost-and-what-a-run-did.html)
- [Automate with clio-coder run](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/exit-codes-and-output.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/ask-several-agents-at-once.html

# Ask several agents at once

> Poll two to five agents on one question and read the vote, or give a council roster one task and let a judge write a single answer.

Sometimes one agent's answer is not enough. `/poll` asks two to five agents the same question independently and shows how they vote. `/council` gives a roster of two to five agents the same task and can have a judge write one answer from theirs. Both are read-only: the members read your project, argue and vote, but never change a file.

**Version scope**

This tutorial describes v0.8.0. The output below is from CLIO Coder run against a fresh CLIO Coder home and a one-file Node package, with one local model (Qwen 3.8 27B) serving every participant. The package's Git status was clean afterwards.

## Before you start

- CLIO Coder connected to at least one model. Every participant can run on the same one.
- For `/council`, a roster in your settings (shown below).
- An interactive session: at the default autonomy level, a poll or a council waits for your approval.

## Ask a quick question with /poll

`/poll` takes the number of participants, then the question. `--options` limits each vote to one of the listed answers, and `--rationale` asks for a short reason with each vote:

```text
/poll --options node:test|vitest|jest --rationale 3 Which test runner should a small dependency-free ES module package like this one use?
```

Without `--models`, every participant runs on your chat model. `--models litellm,big-box/qwen3-coder-next` seats them in turn on the routes you list, so the answers can come from different models. Each participant answers alone: no one sees another's answer.

## Approve the plan

A poll is a small fleet, so at the default autonomy level CLIO Coder shows the plan before anything starts. It names each participant, its agent and its model:

```text
Plan ────────────────────────────── Alt+V shows every field
p1    scout on litellm · qwen3.8-27b
p2    scout on litellm · qwen3.8-27b
p3    scout on litellm · qwen3.8-27b
cost  counts against this session's $5.00 limit
```

Enter allows it, and Esc denies it without starting anyone. At `yolo` the plan runs without this stop. Participants run as the `scout` agent, and every member of a poll or council gets only read-only tools: `read`, `grep`, `find`, `ls`, `git`, `code_nav` and `context`.

## Read the vote

Each participant appears with its time and the start of its answer. When all have voted, CLIO Coder prints the distribution:

```text
poll       3 of 3 voted; majority: node:test
node:test  ### 3 (100%)
```

The headline reads `majority` when one answer has more than half the votes, `plurality` when it leads without a majority, and `tie` when the top two are level. Here all three read `package.json`, saw a `node --test` script and kept it. `/view` opens each full answer. A participant whose vote names none of the options is asked again, with the options quoted.

## Declare a council roster

A council needs a roster. Without one, `/council` stops and says where to add it:

```text
/council needs a roster. Declare one under fleet.rosters in settings.yaml, for example fleet.rosters.default with two to five members, each with a label and a target, then run /council <task> or name another roster with --roster <name>.
```

Each member has a label and a target, and can name a model and an agent. This roster seats one plain reader and one `tester`:

```yaml title=settings.yaml
fleet:
  rosters:
    default:
      members:
        - { label: reader, target: litellm }
        - { label: tester, target: litellm, agent: tester }
```

The roster is read on the next command, without a restart. `--roster <name>` picks another roster. A member whose target runs on an SSH fleet node, or on an agent runtime that cannot enforce read-only tools, such as an ACP peer, is refused before you approve anything.

## Ask the council, with a judge

```text
/council --synthesis judge Is add() in index.js covered by a test, and what is the smallest test that would cover it?
```

The plan card listed `reader` as `scout`, `tester` as `tester`, and a synthesis run as `oracle`. The `tester` member kept its own way of working, but the council's read-only tools still applied, so it argued for a test without writing one. After both answered, the judge read their answers, checked them against the files and wrote one answer. It opened:

```text
Both council members agree on the facts, and my own inspection confirms them:
```

It went on to say that `index.test.js` already imports `add` and checks `add(2,2)` against 4 under `node:test`, so the function is covered.

`--synthesis vote` tallies the members' votes instead, and `none`, the default, returns each answer as it is. `--rounds 2` or `3` shows each member the others' previous answers before it answers again. `--deadline 90s` stops a member that runs too long, and the council returns the rest marked partial.

**What you have**

A spread of independent answers to one question, and for a council either a tally or one written answer with every member's answer behind it. Each member's run has its own sealed run record, and no file in the project changed.

The answers stay out of your main conversation. `/fleet share <runId>` brings one member's answer into it; shared from the synthesis run, it brings the synthesis with every member's labelled answer.

**Boundaries**

- Members on one model are not fully independent. They share its habits, so a unanimous vote from one model is weaker evidence than a split across several. Use `--models` or a mixed roster to spread the question.
- Every member is a model run and counts against your spending limit. Here the `tester` member alone used 22,122 tokens.
- Members run on this machine only. A council never writes files or makes a worktree.

**Next steps**

- [Workers and fleets](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/fleet-dispatch.html)
- [Commands and shortcuts](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/commands-and-modes.html)
- [Coordinate the coding agents you already use](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/coordinate-your-coding-agents.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/system-one-decisions.html

# Can a small decision model improve an agent's work?

> Open questions on System One: evaluating on trajectories, asking better questions, and bringing a decision model, with a first experiment.

Can a small, fast decision model make a coding agent's work better? System One is where CLIO Coder asks that question. You bring a model that answers typed questions, and CLIO Coder gives the agent a `consult` tool, a screen beside the safety judge, and optional triage of queued messages.

The plumbing has shipped. Whether it helps is still open, and the evidence so far is thin.

**Open question, described for 0.8.0**

System One is off until you name a route, and its keys and tool may change between releases. The team, students, and outside researchers are welcome to work on it. All samples below are small, and every experiment on this page is proposed and not yet run.

## The question

Three questions sit inside the big one, and each could come back negative.

- **Trajectories.** With a decision model bound, does the agent take a better path through a task: fewer wrong turns, fewer rounds, and the same or better accepted result?
- **Question formation.** Which questions can a small model answer usefully, and what must the question carry for that to happen?
- **Training.** Could a model trained on agent work outperform a general one on these questions?

## What is measured so far

These were measured on the design 0.6.8 shipped, which 0.8.0 keeps, on small samples. They show what the parts do. None of them shows that System One improves an agent's work.

| Measurement | Result | Sample |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Filter recall on a file digest, on Jev | 0.77, 0.82, 0.92 | Three sets of 6 queries |
| Filter recall on the first 512 characters, on Jev | 0.65, 0.35, 0.92 | The same three sets |
| Filter recall by query type | 0.92 for what a file is for; at best 0.58 for how it behaves | The same sets |
| Judge screen, on a real Haiku judge | Parked 8 of 8 injected pages | 8 pages |
| Judge screen latency | Screen 104 to 157 ms; judge verdict 938 to 1370 ms | The same run |
| Steering triage, how a message relates to the work | 105 of 105 | The relation pick only |
| `consult` calls with Jev bound | 0 calls | 12 real Haiku sessions, 6 with Jev bound |

Read those together. A digest holds up better than a file's opening characters on two of the three sets and ties on the third. It finds what a file is for and misses much of what a file does, which fits a digest that never carries the body.

Precision is weak. Between a third and more than half of filter matches can be wrong, so a filter can narrow a list and cannot settle anything.

### Filter across routes

These also ran on the 0.6.8 design. They are small samples, and the query sets were regression sets, so they were not independent of the work being tested.

| Route | Recall | Precision | Median latency | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Haiku, as a chat route | 0.81 | 0.68 | 2.5 s | Labels |
| Jev | 0.85 | 0.47 | 163 ms | Probabilities |
| A self-hosted chat model | 0.87 | 0.67 | 6.3 s | Labels |

On 3 fresh queries, with about 3 samples, Haiku scored recall 0.83 and precision 1.00, and Jev scored recall 0.50 and precision 0.26. Those figures moved a long way from the table above, which shows how unstable these numbers are. Do not rank the routes from them.

Jev and other engines whose profile declares real probabilities return a score. Any chat route returns one label per question, so its match has no score, and it never drives the judge screen.

### What the screen result covers

The screen result covers injected pages only, and it says nothing about how often the screen would park an honest page.

The most important number is the last row. Given the tool, the agent did not call it once. Nothing has measured a benefit from `consult`, because none of the measured sessions used it on its own.

### One earlier run, on a design that no longer exists

An on/off evaluation ran the older fixed-site design, where CLIO Coder asked its own questions at fixed points in a turn. That design is gone, and so is the run's raw data. Only these numbers remain, so nobody can reanalyze them.

The run used build `jev-1.14.0` with Haiku as the main model, over 24 episodes per arm. Total time with System One on was 1.237 times total time with it off, meaning slower, with an interval of 1.037 to 1.484. Acceptance was 24 of 24 per arm. Hints fired on 4 of 32 turns and changed no rounds.

Do not read that as a verdict on `consult` or on decision models in general. It says that one design cost time and bought nothing visible on that sample.

## Why it matters

A main model is slow and expensive for the small judgments an agent makes constantly: which file to open, whether a web page is trying to instruct it, whether a queued message means stop.

The judge screen numbers show a decision can return in about a tenth of a verdict's time. If small decisions like these can steer the larger model, long agent work gets cheaper and safer.

The clock is a poor measure of that. A decision that adds a second and saves a wrong branch is a win that total time can hide, and a saved second that leads the agent astray is a loss. That is why the direction below is to evaluate on trajectories.

## Directions to work on

### Evaluate on trajectories

Define what a better path means and measure it per episode: rounds, tool calls, files read and then never used, repeated failed commands, cost, and whether the result was accepted. CLIO Coder journals each decision without its content, so the outcome, latency, route, and answering build can be set against the rest of the run.

Agents did not reach for `consult`, so a first result may be about adoption: what tool description or prompting makes an agent use it when it would help, and whether forcing the call helps at all.

### Form better questions

`consult` asks yes-or-no, pick, or rate questions over a small state, and it filters lists against one criterion.

Each engine declares what it can carry, and a question that does not fit abstains instead of being cut down. Open work includes what to put in a digest so that behavior queries improve, how to phrase criteria, and which of an agent's choices are worth asking about.

### Bring a model, and one day train one

You can bring a model today. A server that answers `POST /v1/systemone` becomes a route, and a named capability profile says how its numbers are read. Profiles make no accuracy claim, and there are no fitted thresholds, so a comparison across engines would be new evidence.

Training is an open research direction with no plan or timeline. There is no training data: the decision dataset from earlier releases was removed, and today's journal keeps decision records without content. Building an opt-in dataset is part of the work, including what consent it needs, what to redact, and what counts as a correct label.

## Use CLIO Coder on it today

You need a working chat model, since System One never replaces it, and a route to name. Off is the default and sends nothing.

### Name a route

```sh
clio-coder systemone use jev
clio-coder systemone status
clio-coder systemone check jev --live
```

`status` says what each route reaches and sends. `check --live` sends one content-free decision and reports the build that answered, which shows the route works and says nothing about its quality. In the terminal, `/usage health` shows the same state. A choice takes effect on the next start. For one headless run, pass `--systemone`:

```sh
clio-coder run --systemone jev "<task>"
clio-coder run --systemone off "<task>"
```

### Choose what answers

- `jev` is a hosted engine that needs `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` and returns real probabilities.
- A declared engine is a decision server you run, with a named profile.
- `memory`, `main`, or a chat target answer with one label per question. They have no real probabilities, so a filter match has no score and they never drive the judge screen.

A hosted route receives file digests and heads, chunks of results, web and MCP result text, and queued messages. Redaction is best effort. Use a route you run yourself when that matters.

### Read what happened

```sh
clio-coder telemetry timeline <session-id>
clio-coder telemetry inspect <session-id> --json
```

The timeline includes each System One decision. Use `clio-coder telemetry inspect --run <run-id>` for a dispatched or headless run.

## First experiment

**Proposed, not yet run**

Nobody has run this protocol. If you do, the result is useful whichever way it comes out.

**Score the filter on a repository you know.** This extends the measurements above to new code, adds precision, and needs an afternoon.

### Write the labels before you run anything

Pick a repository you know well. Write 12 queries, six about what a file is for and six about what a file does in its body. For each query, list by hand the files that should match.

### Run each query through `consult`

Ask for the filter form directly, one query per headless run, so the agent's choice not to call the tool does not get in the way:

```sh
clio-coder run --systemone jev "Call consult with a files filter over src/**. Criterion: <query>. Use limit 32. Report the matches and do nothing else."
```

One filter carries at most 256 items and returns at most 32 matches, so scope `paths` to fit and keep each hand-labelled list shorter than that.

### Score it

For each query, compute recall and precision against your labels, separately for the two query types. Note `carried.partial` and which items carried a digest or a head.

### Report it

Open a GitHub issue with the repository's language and size, the build `check --live` reported, your query types, and the scores. Include your sample size and leave out anything private.

Needs: `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` for Jev, or your own decision server. A label route can also run this, though it returns no scores, so a comparison with Jev is a second result.

A natural second experiment, also proposed and not yet run, is a small paired on/off study: the same task and the same model, repeated with `--systemone jev` and `--systemone off`, scored on the trajectory measures above. It needs tasks whose result can be accepted or rejected mechanically, and enough repeats to report an interval.

## How to join

Open a GitHub issue on [the repository](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/issues) saying what you want to try, before or after you run it, and read the [contributor guide](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for code changes. Negative results and replications are welcome.

**Boundaries**

- System One is not a safety net. The deterministic safety rules and the judge decide, the screen can only tighten, and no use removes a confirmation.
- A filter miss is not proof, especially when `carried.partial` is above zero.
- CLIO Coder ships a client for these wires and no inference server.

**Next steps**

- [System One guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/system-one.html)
- [Can an agent run be a scientific record?](https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/sealed-run-records.html)
- [Let CLIO Coder work without watching every call](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/let-it-work-with-containment-and-rewind.html)

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/sealed-run-records.html

# Can an agent run be a scientific record?

> What a sealed run record proves and what it cannot, how far repeated runs differ, and a first experiment to measure that spread with CLIO Coder.

What would it take to treat an agent run as a scientific record that someone else can check? CLIO Coder already writes a sealed record of each run. Nobody has yet studied what those records can support as evidence, how much two runs of one task differ, or what a reader in another lab would still need.

**Open question, described for v0.8.0**

The records and commands on this page have shipped. The research use of them is new. No reproducibility study exists yet, so this page has no outcome numbers, and every experiment here is proposed and not yet run. The team, students, and outside researchers are welcome.

## The question

- **Repeatability.** Given the same task, repository, and model, how far apart are the results of repeated runs, and which recorded facts explain the difference?
- **Sufficiency.** What must a shared record contain before an outside reader can judge a claim about a run without re-running it?
- **Method.** Can sealed records carry a controlled comparison between agent configurations well enough to publish?

## What is known so far

These are facts about the design, read from the source at this version. They are not study results.

A finished run writes its settlement, its result object, and an assessment, then seals them. A seal records a SHA-256 hash chain over the journal, plus the size and hash of every journal segment and stored object. `clio-coder telemetry verify` checks all of that using only the scope's own files, so it works on any machine.

**What a seal shows.** The record's files match their manifest and the chain is intact, so damage and partial edits are caught.

**What a seal does not show.** The chain is unkeyed and carries no signature, so someone with the files could write a consistent new record, and a seal cannot say who produced it. Verification also runs nothing. A verified seal says the record is intact, and leaves open whether the agent's work was correct or would come out the same again.

Other parts of the design matter to a researcher:

- Unknowns stay unknown. A missing token count reads as not recorded instead of zero, and a dropped or refused record leaves a gap record behind.
- An assessment keeps trust states separately, including whether a run's claims were grounded in commands that actually ran.
- Sharing has four profiles. `content-free` is the default, `structural` adds structure such as prompt and tool-schema manifests, `report` is structural with target ids anonymized too, for an archive linked from a public issue, and `research` adds content captured under consent.
- A share re-applies secret redaction, and below `research` it keeps only allowlisted fields and anonymizes identities. Redaction is best effort.

## Why it matters

A success rate and a description of the setup leave a reader unable to see what an agent did, what it cost, or which results were lost along the way. A record format that keeps those facts, and says plainly when one is missing, could raise the standard of evidence.

Every other page in this section depends on the answer. A study of decision models, memory, or compaction is only as good as the records behind it, and the variance between repeated runs sets how many episodes such a study needs.

## Directions to work on

**Measure run-to-run variance.** Model output varies, and so does what the agent chooses to read. A baseline spread for rounds, cost, and accepted results on a few task types would give every later study its sample size.

**Decide what provenance needs.** An unkeyed chain suits integrity on your own machine. A shared claim may need more, such as a signature or a published digest. Designing that, and testing whether it is worth its cost, is open work.

**Test what a reader can conclude.** Give someone a `content-free` archive and a claim. Find out which claims they can check, which need `structural` or `research`, and what is still missing.

**Build the analysis layer.** CLIO Coder exposes JSON reads over its journals, and it has no comparison tool. A small script that folds two sets of runs into a paired table would help every study here.

## Use CLIO Coder on it today

### Run a task and read its record

```sh
clio-coder run --agent <agent-id> --json "<task>"
clio-coder telemetry inspect --run <run-id> --json
clio-coder telemetry cost --run <run-id> --json
```

`clio-coder agents` lists the agents. For a supported local or OpenAI-compatible runtime, `--temperature` sets the sampler for one run. The JSON stream ends with a result frame, and the run has its own scope.

### Verify it

```sh
clio-coder telemetry verify --run <run-id>
clio-coder fleet verify <run-id> --json
```

`telemetry verify` reports the seal. `fleet verify` also reads the settlement and reports the mismatch kind when a seal fails.

### Share it

```sh
clio-coder telemetry share --run <run-id> --profile content-free --dry-run
clio-coder telemetry share --run <run-id> --profile content-free --out run.tar.gz
clio-coder telemetry verify run.tar.gz
```

Nothing is uploaded. Read the `--dry-run` output before you send an archive to anyone. On another machine, `clio-coder telemetry import run.tar.gz` verifies the archive and places it for reading.

### Capture more, deliberately

```sh
clio-coder telemetry consent --workspace <dir>
```

Set `telemetry.mode: research` and turn on the `telemetry.research` flags you need. Content capture also needs consent for that workspace. Research capture is capped at 256 MiB per session, and a refusal leaves a gap record.

## First experiment

**Proposed, not yet run**

Nobody has run this protocol. If you do, the spread you measure is the first baseline this project has.

**Measure the spread of one small task.**

### Fix the setup

Choose a small repository with a test suite, and a task whose result those tests can accept or reject. Commit the starting state. Fix the model, route, and CLIO Coder version, and write them down.

### Run it ten times

Run the task ten times, each from a clean checkout of the same commit. Pass `--temperature 0` as well if your route supports it, then repeat the set without it if you have the budget.

### Fold the records

For each run, read `telemetry inspect --run <run-id> --json` and `telemetry cost --run <run-id> --json`. Tabulate tool calls, tokens, cost, duration, stop reason, and whether the tests accepted the result. Report the median and the range.

### Check it from outside

Share two runs with `--profile content-free`, then give the archives and your table to a colleague on another machine. Record what they could verify and what they had to take on trust.

### Report it

Open a GitHub issue with the setup, the table, and your colleague's notes. Ten runs is a small sample, so say so.

Needs: any chat route and a repository with tests. A local model server avoids API keys and spend. A second machine is only needed for the last step.

## How to join

Open a GitHub issue on [the repository](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/issues) saying what you want to try, before or after you run it, and read the [contributor guide](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for code changes. Negative results and replications are welcome.

**Boundaries**

- A seal shows integrity of the record. It is not proof of correctness, authorship, or repeatability.
- Share profiles reduce what leaves your machine, and redaction is best effort, so read what you are about to share.
- Publish numbers and methods. Do not attach another person's session content without their agreement.

**Next steps**

- [See what a session cost and what a run did](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/see-what-a-session-cost-and-what-a-run-did.html)
- [Can a small decision model improve an agent's work?](https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/system-one-decisions.html)
- [All open questions](https://coder.iowarp.ai/research.html)
